blocks.text: Master Huiming: A Brief Introduction

inline.s: Master Huiming (

) was a great monk of the late Qing and early Republic and a native of Fujian. Much like the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, he cut an unremarkable figure and had no formal schooling; yet through strict observance of the precepts, arduous practice, long journeys on foot, and broad learning crowned by solitary awakening, he finally fathomed the Way. Thereupon his wisdom opened wide and his literary thought gushed like a spring; he mounted the Dharma seat and poured down sweet rain. At the age of thirty-two he expounded the Lotus Sutra at Fayu Temple. His views were original and his explanations penetrating, so his fame spread far and his karmic affinity for lecturing grew ever richer. Students gathered beneath his seat from every quarter, and Mount Putuo, Tiantong Temple, and Lingyin Temple were his chief places of propagating the Dharma. The Master was skilled in expounding the Dharma without clinging to words and phrases; his dwelling was plain and simple, his style lofty, and all his life he firmly upheld the practice of Chan. So broad was his Dharma affinity and so deep his transformative influence that he won the deep reverence of the worthy men of his day and was counted among the eminent elders of Shanghai and Hangzhou in the early Republic. For more than ten years he served as abbot of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou. In the nineteenth year of the Republic (1930) he passed into quiescence at Lingyin Temple, aged seventy-one by worldly reckoning and sixty-three in monastic years. He left behind the book Record of Master Huiming's Teachings.

blocks.text: The Origin of This Compilation

inline.s: Our Master has been spreading the Dharma in the Jianghan region for over four years now. We who attend upon him at his seat have received a word or half a verse from him, like seeds splitting their husks in the fields, brushed by the spring wind without knowing that we were being nourished. In earlier days we gathered up the essentials of his teaching and compiled them into a record of sayings, so that in the intervals between his talks we might draw inspiration from them. Yet because his words were terse and their meaning far-reaching, it was hard to pluck out what was subtle and hidden, and we trembled for fear of failing to gain right knowledge and right view. In the autumn of the yihai year (1935), the Master returned from Nanjing. After we had paid our respects, we all thought of how we might be benefited, and pressed him on every side for instruction. The Master said: “The Buddha Dharma has no fixed teaching that can be spoken; in the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, only awakening and realization matter, and talk is not esteemed. If within the Dharma that is beyond words one insists on expressing it in words, then the words too become a trap and a snare. One who can grasp this purport may as well expound it in skillful means, to spur on practice in actual fact. But to cling to the trap and the snare is to lose the meaning of the school.” We all assented. When his perfect voice spread abroad, every phrase held many flavors, every teaching gathered back into the one mind, and the great purport of the mind-ground Dharma was wholly present in them. As for his skillful guidance, his meaning went from the shallow to the deep, while his language made the deep plain to the shallow; he neither clung to the scriptures nor departed from them. Thereupon those who held to the teachings were ashamed, as though gazing at flowers through mist, and for the first time could tell root from stem; while beginners rejoiced that, having lost their way in a far and desolate corner, they suddenly knew the road home. When the talks were over, all praised with one voice. Fellow students in distant places had been kept from that excellent gathering. All agreed that, as when a waterfall hangs from a sheer cliff and its sound is heard across the gorge, or when the moon stands in mid-heaven and its image appears in ten thousand streams, without a record how could the flame be passed from torch to torch? Without committing it to the printing blocks, how could the meal be shared? Letters came in one after another, all saying the same thing. The Master saw their sincerity and gave his consent. So the talks were gathered into a volume and published under the title Record of Instructions. It was meant so that those who had been present might take the sound into their ears and make it a cause, and those who had not been present might likewise grasp the meaning through the words. Yet I, Yaozhi, am deficient in practice and shallow in learning; I cannot look up and see the moon to which my Master's finger points, and so I find it hard to paint the music of the harp upon his fingertips. Now that the writing is done, my shame and awe are great; I set down reverently how it began and ended, to make clear the occasion of this compilation.

The trap and the snare (quanti): quan is a bamboo basket for catching fish; ti is a net for catching hares. Later, “trap and snare” came to mean the means or instrument by which an end is reached. Zhuangzi says: “The basket exists for the sake of the fish; once you have the fish, you forget the basket. The snare exists for the sake of the hare; once you have the hare, you forget the snare.”
Reverently recorded by the disciple Chen Yaozhi, in the spring of the bingzi year (1936).

blocks.text: First Sitting: Faith, Vow, and Practice

inline.s: Fellow students! The Chan school takes “mind itself is Buddha” as the ultimate, and therefore does not rely on written or spoken words; hence it is said that “the path of speech is cut off, the road of mental activity is extinguished.” The principle of the Esoteric Dharma is even more beyond speech. Now, because you have asked again and again, and because each of you has practiced for years and already has some understanding of this method, I shall follow the conditions and speak of it in skillful means. My only wish is that you come to know the process of learning the Buddha Dharma, as a spur to your practice. I hope you will listen with pure minds and give rise to no discrimination; for as soon as discrimination arises, views and opinions are born. The phrase “mind itself is Buddha” is the root of the Chan school; wherever the teaching goes, it cannot be left behind, because all is mind only.

The path of speech is cut off, the road of mental activity is extinguished: the Way is beyond speech and thought; therefore when speech begins the Way is cut off, and when mental activity begins the road is extinguished.

The three words faith, vow, and practice carry the meaning of advancing step by step, yet students often pass over them carelessly without reflection. You should know that within these three words, each single word has its own processes and its own degrees. Among the fellow students seated here, some understand the doctrines and some have only just aroused the aspiration; so let me explain briefly the processes and degrees of faith, vow, and practice as follows.

The ocean of Buddha Dharma can be entered only by faith; therefore the word faith must first be taken to heart. But faith differs as true or false, and in between one must pass through many stages. If these stages are not clearly understood, one cannot avoid confusing the true with the false, turning back in regret midway, or meeting with other deviations. The stages of faith, put simply, are the following.

1. Unbelief. Sentient beings are inherently endowed with the Buddha-nature, no different from the Buddha, but it is screened by the karmic force of many kalpas; hence at the outset they do not believe in the Buddha Dharma. Later, gradually urged by relatives and friends, or moved for a time by outer circumstances, they harbor the thought of giving it a try. At this stage they appear to be learning the Buddha Dharma, but in their minds faith has not truly arisen.

2. Doubting faith. What is doubting faith? To doubt is to be uncertain through confusion. The beginner believes on one side and doubts on the other. Today he feels that learning the Buddha Dharma is good; tomorrow he feels it is not. Today he meets a person of good conditions who praises it, and his faith increases; tomorrow he meets a person of bad conditions who laughs at it as superstition, and doubt arises again. He is at odds with himself. Such faith is called doubting faith. Where, then, does this doubt come from? You should know that it still arises from one's own mind. Ask your own mind: if faith has already arisen, why does doubt arise as well? Faith is the stirring of the true mind; doubt is born of karmic force. The karmic force of sentient beings is too heavy, so that the moment a single thought of the true mind is about to arise, boundless karmic force comes to block it and will not allow the student to arouse faith and practice. This is still the crucial moment of battle between Buddha and Mara — how dangerous it is! Therefore one must cut off doubt before faith can arise.

3. Shallow faith. After some time of conditioning, the beginner gains a little understanding of the Buddha Dharma; doubt diminishes and faith arises, but the aspiration is not genuine and the faith is shallow. Perhaps he seeks some worldly hope, or seeks breadth of knowledge and much learning. This is ordinary faith, and it cannot generate the power of vow and practice. Why? Because his faith is shallow: when the benefits fail to appear, or circumstances change, he casts his faith beyond the nine clouds. Such faith is like a feather in the air — one gust of wind, and no one knows where it has blown.

4. Deep faith. Having practiced for a good while, the student has gained some benefit and feels that the Buddha Dharma is the truth; he devotes himself to practice with a resolve that does not change. Yet this cannot be called true understanding; it may only be called grass on a wall — it has roots, but once the wind blows it still bends both ways. That is, though the foundation of faith in the Buddha is laid, faith in the teacher and the Dharma is not yet firm: today he takes refuge with this Dharma master to study Chan, tomorrow he takes refuge with that guru to study Esoteric. Clinging to objects, he gives rise to thoughts; seeing something different, he thinks of changing. This comes of not understanding that one's own mind is Buddha, and of not knowing the principle of penetrating deeply through one gate.

5. Settled faith. Settled faith is firm and unwavering faith. When the student has practiced to this point, having been conditioned for a long time and with karmic obstructions gradually dissolving, his faith may be called firm. Like a great tree with deep roots, it cannot be shaken by the wind. In the teacher and the Dharma he has faith, one and without a second; he advances bravely and diligently, and does not give rise to weariness. But when the wind is strong, even a great tree can still be shaken. If a practitioner's root karmic obstructions are stirred up, and outward circumstances press upon him, his faith still cannot escape some variation. Therefore settled faith is still not ultimate.

6. True faith. True faith is faith that accords with true suchness. True suchness is thus and unmoving, pure and markless. When faith reaches this point it is called true faith. True faith does not move; it is like space itself, and nothing can shake it. At this point one's own mind, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the teacher are mind sealing mind, breath linked to breath, without the slightest trace and without the least discrimination. Therefore the Diamond Sutra says: “When the mind of faith is pure, then the mark of reality is produced.” Only when faith reaches this realm is it true faith, and only true faith is ultimate.

Judged by the stages of faith described above, the analysis may seem excessive. In truth, unless these differences are clearly analyzed, true faith cannot arise. How can one become true? By removing the false one becomes true. So removing the false is the most important and most direct work. Yet how easy is it to remove the false? If you want to make it easy, it is best to begin with speech. The character for faith, xin, is built from the element for “person” and the element for “words,” which shows people where to begin. You may think that this word faith means the faithfulness of worldly dealings — what has it to do with the faith of the Buddha Dharma? You should know that the Buddha Dharma is not apart from worldly dharmas: words arise from the mind, and a person stands by his word. This is why I, Huiming, formerly asked you all to keep the precept of making heart and mouth one, and my intent lay precisely here.

Do not slight the four words “heart and mouth as one”; this precept is the practical work of removing the false and establishing faith. The Buddha required the bhikṣus to confess their own faults — precisely to prove their faith. The Confucians likewise speak of “being true to one's word” and “faithful in speech,” which also teach people to build the foundation of faith through speech. Take the world of commerce: there are old firms of several hundred years whose goods are dearer than others', yet their business flourishes and never declines. Other shops sell more cheaply, and people trust them the less. Why is this? Because one keeps a single honest price, with goods genuine and the price fair, while the other shouts a price to the sky and haggles down to the ground — there is deceit in it. This one point alone proves that only when word and deed are not two can faith be established. And it shows all the more the benefit of the word faith.

In worldly teachings it is said, “Without trustworthiness a people cannot stand.” In the Buddha Dharma it is said, “Faith is the mother of merit.” This shows plainly that faith is the root of both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. I hope each of you will constantly examine himself as to whether his heart and mouth are one and whether he is true to his word. Never talk at random, never promise lightly and keep faith lightly. Once one's credibility is lost, one does not even have the ground to stand on as a human being — how much less can one speak of learning the Buddha Dharma?

Next, the word vow. Whatever one undertakes, one must first have a vow; without a vow nothing can be accomplished, and so it is called the power of vow. Only when there is a wish can a power arise; only with power can one press forward. Therefore once faith is present, one should at once make vows. But vows differ as small vows, empty vows, true vows, and great vows.

What is a small vow? Beginners in the Buddha Dharma mostly seek only their own benefit, and their vow-power is small. Small vows may be briefly described as three kinds. First, seeking glory and pleasure in this life — that is, seeking fame, profit, blessing, and long life, and even wife, wealth, children, and emolument. Second, seeking blessings in the next life — that is, seeking to be reborn as a human or a deva in the next life, to gain great wealth and honor and enjoy happiness. Third, seeking only one's own liberation and clinging to nirvāṇa. They little realize that fame and profit, respect, wife and wealth, children and emolument are all the result of our own defiled good causes from past kalpas; they need not be sought at all. Even if they are obtained, life is like a dream, and in the blink of an eye all is empty. To be reborn as a human or a deva with wealth, honor, and happiness is still within saṃsāra, and one cannot escape the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death. Hence the Sixth Patriarch said: “You may think to cultivate blessings to wipe out your offenses; but when a later life wins blessings, the offense is still there.” All of these are small vows. And those who vainly seek nirvāṇa, wishing only for their own liberation, do not know that the Tathāgata came into the world to save the world and deliver living beings. If one knows only self-liberation and not the benefiting of others, one is clinging to a barren void, and that too is a small vow.

What is an empty vow? An empty vow is like a bad check that cannot be cashed. Though the student of the Buddha Dharma may have faith, the obstruction of karmic consciousness is still deep. Now and then, stirred by emotion and excited for the moment, he lightly makes a vow, while heart and mouth still do not correspond. The vow is no sooner spoken than he turns and forgets it. Or he merely shows off with words to win empty fame. Making vows in this way not only makes one liable to fall into false speech, but adds the grave offense of breaking one's vow.

What is a true vow? It is a vow that is real and not vain. Whether great or small, it comes from utmost sincerity and has been carefully weighed; once the vow is made, in the stirring of the mind and the arising of thoughts one dares not be careless, and whatever circumstances arise, one remains as before to the end and never goes against it. For example, if one vows to be affectionate toward one's fellow practitioners, one hides their faults and makes known their virtues, and meets every matter with compliance. If one vows to give rise to no hatred, then in all things one is gentle and harmonious, affliction does not arise, and gradually one comes to treat friend and foe as equal. But such a vow, though true, is not great — though it brings benefit, it is still not ultimate.

What is a great vow? When conditions have ripened for the student of the Buddha Dharma and he meets a good teacher, thoroughly understands the true meaning of the Buddha Dharma, and knows deeply how hard it is to repay the Buddha's grace, he arouses a mind of utmost sincerity that is not two and makes the great vow to benefit others without self, to spread the Dharma and benefit living beings, and to vow that until all living beings are saved he will not be saved himself. As for giving up one's body for the Dharma and expending all one's wealth and life, that comes second. This is what is meant by a vast and mighty vow.

Everyone should know that the mind of vow is the mind of cause; only with a mind of cause is there the fruition of awakening. Great cause, great fruit; true cause, true fruit — as it is said, the cause embraces the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. Not only must one who studies the Buddha Dharma make vows in order to bring forth fruit from the cause; even a policy or a proposal, or a technique or an invention, must first rest on a correct insight. And having gained correct insight, one must still have a firm vow, shrinking from no hardship or danger and never turning back through a hundred setbacks, before the goal can be reached. If one has no settled view in one's breast, one certainly cannot succeed; and if the vow-power is not firm, one's spirit will surely scatter, and in the end one will still fail. There are many such cases; there is no need to list them in detail. In self-benefit the student of the Buddha Dharma seeks to understand the mind and see the nature; in benefiting others he seeks to save the world and deliver living beings. Saving the world and delivering living beings is indeed hard, and understanding the mind and seeing the nature is no quick achievement either; therefore one must make a true and great vow. Our making of vows is the same as taking an oath, and so it is called a sworn vow. Whoever goes against it must surely suffer severe retribution.

Next, the word practice. From the very beginning the student of the Buddha Dharma must practice — that is, act in accordance with the Dharma. But practice is rooted in vow. Once a true vow of the mind has been made, one should put it into practice according to the vow. If there is a vow but no practice, or the practice lacks strength, it is like talking about a king's banquet without getting a single bite. Therefore, whatever the size of the vow, whether for self-cultivation or for benefiting others, one must be able to do what is hard to do and endure what is hard to endure, sparing not even the shattering of one's body into powder, and never wavering until the practice fulfills the vow. But the scope of the word practice is very broad; put simply, it means to walk the bodhisattva path. The bodhisattva path is the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices. Yet the ten thousand practices do not go beyond the six pāramitās. According to the Buddha's teaching: by giving one saves others from stinginess and greed; by keeping the precepts one saves them from transgression; by patience one saves them from hatred; by diligence one saves them from indolence; by meditative concentration one saves them from distraction; and by prajñā one saves them from delusion. These six pāramitās all contain the meaning of saving oneself and saving others and of crossing over together to the other shore, which is precisely the meaning of the word practice. But of saving others and saving oneself, which comes first? You should know that self and others are one body, and that benefiting both self and others — how can there be a before and after? For to save others is to save oneself, and to save oneself is precisely to save others. The bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle has no mark of self and no mark of persons, and so knows only the benefit of others. Just because he knows only the benefit of others, in the end, before living beings are all saved, he himself is saved first. The bodhisattva of the Small Vehicle clings to the mark of self and the mark of persons and knows only self-benefit. Just because he knows only self-benefit, his grasping at self is hard to break, and in the end he is not easily saved himself. From this one may know: benefiting oneself without benefiting others, one is still on this shore; benefiting others without a self is the other shore.

In sum, the three words faith, vow, and practice all arise from the mind. Now that you are studying the mind-ground Dharma, you must work in the mind at every moment. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch taught people, first: “This must be practiced in the mind”; and again: “The deluded speak with the mouth, the wise practice in the mind.” He also said: “To recite with the mouth while the mind does not practice is to be turned by the sutra.” I hope you will arouse faith according to the mind, make vows according to the mind, and practice with strength according to the mind. The mind is true suchness; true suchness means true and not vain, thus and unmoving. If thought after thought one can rely on such a mind, then one accomplishes true faith, true vow, and true practice. The mind is originally immeasurable, its essence great and without outside; if in every place one can rely on such a mind, then one accomplishes great faith, great vow, and great practice. Being both true and great, naturally mind and Buddha share one body, and response and correspondence meet.

What I, Huiming, have said is rather coarse and shallow. Yet though the words are coarse, they are not without deep meaning. Which of the ancient worthies of the Chan school did not understand the teachings? Which of them did not use coarse and simple language to instruct students? The reason they did so was their fear that students might leave their own mind and nature behind and waste effort on the mere words and phrases of the scriptures, only increasing the obstruction of theory.

blocks.text: Second Sitting: Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom

inline.s: Fellow students, last time I spoke of faith, vow, and practice; today I shall speak of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. These six words — faith, vow, practice, precepts, concentration, wisdom — are the most important foundation for one who studies the Buddha Dharma, and they cannot be separated. For only with true faith, vow, and practice can one speak of precepts, concentration, and wisdom; and only by keeping the precepts, cultivating concentration, and giving rise to wisdom can one have true faith, vow, and practice.

The Chan school takes “mind itself is Buddha” as its root, and everything must be worked out in the mind. The mind takes no-mark as its mark; so today I shall speak of the markless precepts, concentration, and wisdom. But since it is called markless, why speak of precepts, concentration, and wisdom at all? This is what the Sixth Patriarch meant by untying the bonds according to the case. For the karmic consciousness of living beings is very heavy, and without skillful means how could they enter deeply? Therefore the student of the Buddha Dharma must begin by keeping the precepts; only by keeping the precepts can he cultivate concentration and give rise to wisdom.

What are the precepts? When the mind-ground is without wrong, that is the precepts of self-nature. Precepts are of two kinds, with mark and without mark: those with mark are called bodily precepts, those without mark are called mind precepts. One who cultivates the mind-ground Dharma should strictly keep the mind precepts. Your sitting in meditation now is precisely the work of the mind precepts. Why? Because after you take the seat, you concentrate single-mindedly on the mantra, and by the power of the mantra all deluded thoughts are locked out. When after a long time deluded thoughts no longer arise, that is the realm of a mind-ground without wrong. Not only when on the seat is it so; after leaving the seat it is still so. At all times and in all places, giving rise to no discrimination and no affliction, naturally one is one and the same in motion and in stillness — only then is the precept of a mind-ground without wrong fulfilled. Though the realm of the mind precepts is very high, if one can truly arouse the aspiration and has true faith, vow, and practice, what difficulty is there? But since karmic force is not yet dissolved and the power of concentration is insufficient, one easily gives rise to thoughts on meeting objects and the mind is turned by circumstances. So it is better also to keep the precepts with mark; that is more beneficial. I hope you will consult the eight articles for breaking through the gate that were set down earlier (see Appendix One, “The Secret Essentials of Breaking Through the Gate”) and carefully realize which belong to the aspect of practice and which to the aspect of mind. The aspect of practice is the precepts with mark; the aspect of mind is the precepts without mark. To go from the aspect of practice to the aspect of mind in the precepts is to reach the markless precepts from the precepts with mark. You should know that keeping the precepts is the most important matter in the Buddha Dharma; whatever the school or sect, all give weight to the precepts. The Confucians too have the three things a gentleman guards against and Yanzi's four prohibitions. And since the Buddha Dharma includes both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, one certainly cannot enter the gate without keeping the precepts. In recent times the Buddha Dharma in China has not flourished because students have failed to observe bodily and mental precepts in practice, and so they have drawn people's doubt and slander. We should urgently set an example ourselves and strive to work at the word precepts. Take a mind-ground without wrong as the root of the precepts, benefiting others without self as right practice, and the eight articles for breaking through the gate as the spur; guard the body from reckless action and guard the mind from reckless movement. In time the waters of concentration clear, and the pearl of the mind appears of itself.

What is concentration? When the mind-ground is without thought, that is the concentration of self-nature. In studying the Buddha Dharma the main thing is to attain samādhi; samādhi means right concentration. How can right concentration be attained? It requires that not one thought arise. The sutra says: “When the mind of faith is pure, then the mark of reality is produced.” The mark of reality is thus and unmoving, and unmoving is concentration. If a single thought stirs, then ignorance and affliction rise along with it, and the mind is no longer settled. Therefore it is said that a mind-ground without thought is concentration. Just because there is no thought, it is called right thought; and all virtues are complete, and all wisdom naturally appears before one. Fellow students! Not only must a student of the Buddha Dharma have the power of concentration so as not to be troubled by Mara or moved by circumstances; even in worldly affairs nothing can succeed without the power of concentration. It is said that wealth and honor cannot corrupt him, poverty and lowliness cannot move him, and power and force cannot bend him — this is what the power of concentration brings about. The power of concentration comes from cultivation. All those from ancient times whose merit benefited the world and whose names have come down through ten thousand generations were men who devoted themselves to cultivation. Take Zhuge Liang: his whole life's achievement was accomplished through the four words “tranquility brings far-reaching vision.” Tranquility is the concentration gained through cultivation, and far-reaching is the wisdom gained through tranquility.

What is wisdom? When the mind-ground is without self, that is the wisdom of self-nature. Our own mind-Buddha has immeasurable wonderful function, inconceivable. Only because the deluded do not know that the four elements are fundamentally illusory do they take the false self too seriously, and thus screen off the true self of original prajñā, the supreme wisdom. The first thing for a student of the Buddha Dharma is to break the mark of self; for when there is the mark of self, there are the marks of person, of living beings, and of a life span. If there is no mark of self, then there are no marks at all, and this very body is empty and still; all wisdom naturally appears before one, and one can cross beyond all suffering and distress. Therefore it is said that a mind-ground without self is the wisdom of self-nature. Look at the ancient worthies, and at the sages and heroes of the world — which of them did not come by it through no-self? Even a martyr who gives up his life, or a chaste wife who dies with her husband, because in a single thought they had no such false self, could sacrifice themselves for benevolence and give up their lives for righteousness, and their names have come down through a thousand ages. If a student of the Buddha Dharma wishes the pearl's light to appear and great wisdom to arise, he should first break his grasping at self. The verse says:
All dharmas are one mind alone — a makeshift name, a phantom thrown.
The self is not the awakened ground; in marklessness the truth is found.

Fellow students! Though the Dharma gates of the Buddha Dharma are many, none falls outside the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Only, within the three vehicles, the realms of the three studies differ. As the Sixth Patriarch told Zhicheng: “Your teacher's precepts, concentration, and wisdom are for those of small capacity; my precepts, concentration, and wisdom are for those of great capacity.” For the essence of precepts, concentration, and wisdom is the same, but their function differs, and so their realms differ. The way of the three studies is not only so in the Buddha Dharma; the Confucians are the same: to subdue the self and return to propriety, so that all under heaven return to benevolence — that is the gradual order of the three studies. For to subdue the self is to remove the desires of things, which is precepts. To return to propriety is to restore one's original nature; the original nature is unmoving, and unmoving is concentration. All under heaven returning to benevolence is wonderful function without end, which is wisdom. From this one sees that in worldly and world-transcending dharmas the principle is not two, because all is mind only. Furthermore, in the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, precepts contain concentration, concentration contains wisdom, and wisdom contains precepts. As it is said, one yet three, three yet one, and none of them goes outside one's own mind. If the student can truly understand his own mind, he will naturally awaken to the markless precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

blocks.text: Third Sitting: The Fourfold Refuge

inline.s: Fellow students! In the fourfold refuge there is the refuge with mark and the refuge without mark. What I speak of today is the refuge without mark. The Buddha Dharma is divided into the exoteric and the esoteric: those who study the exoteric teachings take refuge in the Three Jewels — Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; those who study the esoteric teachings add, beyond the Three Jewels, a refuge in the teacher, because the esoteric Dharma is supreme and gives weight to the guru. But all of these are refuges with mark. The markless fourfold refuge that I, Huiming, speak of is based on the principle of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric. I shall now explain it briefly in order.

Taking refuge in the Buddha: in which Buddha do we take refuge? If we take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, Śākyamuni Buddha has already entered nirvāṇa. If we take refuge in Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha is in the West. If we take refuge in the buddhas of the ten directions, the buddhas of the ten directions are immeasurable. If we take refuge in a Buddha carved of wood, molded of clay, or embroidered in thread, such a Buddha only represents the Dharma and has no consciousness. In which Buddha, then, do we ultimately take refuge? You should know that Buddha means awakened. Buddha and living beings are fundamentally without difference; there is only the distinction of awakened and unawakened. The student of the Buddha Dharma uses the initial awakening to awaken the original awakening. But initial awakening and original awakening are not apart from one's own mind. Therefore taking refuge in the Buddha is taking refuge in the awakening of one's own mind, not in a Buddha outside the mind. But is there a Buddha outside the mind? The answer is that there certainly is. Though Śākyamuni Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, in truth he has not entered nirvāṇa; though Amitābha Buddha is in the West, his dharmakāya, like those of all the buddhas of the ten directions, is immeasurable and all-pervading. But though the buddhas are immeasurable and all-pervading, if our own minds are unawakened, what have the buddhas to do with us? Only when our own mind is constantly awake do we meet in response with the buddhas of the ten directions. Therefore taking refuge in the Buddha is taking refuge in the awakening of one's own mind.

Taking refuge in the Dharma: the Dharma gates of the Buddha Dharma are immeasurable and every dharma is equal; in which dharma do we ultimately take refuge? You should know that dharma means right. To take refuge in the Dharma is to take refuge in rightness. The student of the Buddha Dharma must possess right knowledge and right view, and establish right speech and right action. What is right? Purity and compassion are right; a mind-ground without wrong is right; benefiting others without self is right; no-thought and no-mark are right. But purity and compassion, and even marklessness, as well as the Buddha's teaching of the Noble Eightfold Path, all do not go outside one's own mind: when the mind is right, all is right — as it is said, one is all. Therefore taking refuge in the Dharma is taking refuge in the rightness of one's own mind.

Taking refuge in the Saṅgha: the original meaning of saṅgha is a multitude of bhikṣus dwelling together in harmony. But the saṅgha of the past cannot be seen; the saṅgha of the present is many, and eminent monks are not few; in which saṅgha do we ultimately take refuge? You should know that saṅgha means pure. To take refuge in the Saṅgha is to take refuge in purity. Our own minds are originally pure, but through many kalpas the habits of defilement have grown deep, so that the numinous clarity is obscured, and we create karma and suffer. From now on we must sweep away all seeds of affliction and habit, so that not a speck of dust defiles us, and restore our original pure face. Therefore taking refuge in the Saṅgha is taking refuge in the purity of one's own mind.

Taking refuge in the teacher: when the student of the Buddha Dharma is deluded, the teacher saves him; when awakened, he saves himself. All living beings differ in five natures. As for ordinary beings of undetermined nature, when they meet the Great Vehicle they study the Great Vehicle, when they meet the Small Vehicle they study the Small Vehicle, and when they meet outer paths they study outer paths. The relation to a teacher is therefore of the greatest importance. But this speaks of a teacher with mark, not a teacher without mark. The teacher without mark is one's own mind. Why? Because one's own mind is originally complete with virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and is one body with all the buddhas. If one abandons one's own mind and seeks only outwardly for a teacher with mark, then even if one meets a clear teacher, if one does not constantly examine and observe one's own mind, how can one meet the teacher's mind in response? You have come to me to study the Dharma; if you take my physical body as your teacher, how does my physical body differ from yours? In my recorded sayings it is plainly said that the mystery lies in transmitting mind by mind; since it is called mystery, it cannot be the fleshly heart. For the fleshly heart clings deludedly and screens the numinous knowing. Since it is called mind-transmission, it cannot be spoken in words. This mysterious mind is precisely your original mind, the fruit-body of the buddhas of the three times, the true cause of the buddhahood of all living beings, and the one and only true teacher for us. Therefore taking refuge in the teacher is taking refuge in the teacher that is one's own mind.

In sum, in the fourfold refuge the Buddha is awakening, the Dharma is rightness, the Saṅgha is purity, and the teacher is mind. If you string these four words together and read them forward and backward, you have awakening, rightness, purity, mind; mind, purity, rightness, awakening. From this you may awaken to the truth that only with awakening and rightness can the mind be pure, and that when the mind is pure one attains right awakening. Taking refuge in awakening, rightness, purity, and mind is all taking refuge in one's own mind. Day after day you recite the fourfold refuge without knowing that its principle is just this. The deluded always seek on marks and do not realize within their own minds. You should know that in seeking outside the mind, the exoteric teachings have the three baskets, so many, and the esoteric Dharma has five divisions, so elaborate — where, then, would you begin to practice and study? Our Buddha appeared in the world precisely for the one great matter of “mind itself is Buddha.” The ancient worthies of the Chan school inherited the mind-Dharma, and so their merit is boundless. In studying the Buddha Dharma we should apply ourselves to our own minds; only thus do we accord with the Buddha's intent.

Fellow students! The fourfold refuge too is spoken in skillful means. It is like a key handed to you to open a lock; once the lock is open you will naturally see the treasure of your own mind. But those who cannot awaken to the markless fourfold refuge keep turning about on marks. If when first arousing the aspiration, or when practicing, or when bowing to the Buddha in repentance, one is aware, yet in the turning of a thought one is unaware again — such awareness is a deluded awareness with roots, not true awareness. I hope you will cut off all these deluded, discriminating, mark-clinging thoughts as a sharp knife cuts through tangled hemp, and work solely on your own mind, beginning from awareness. To let go of awareness with mark and awaken to awareness without mark is true self-awakening.

Next, rightness. Only when you have awareness can you be right; if you are unaware, you are not right. Not right is crooked, and when crooked, precepts, concentration, and wisdom cannot be spoken of, nor faith, vow, and practice; what then of the fourfold refuge? As for worldly dharmas, conduct that accords with law and morality is right, and otherwise not right; to choose the good and follow it is right, and the unwholesome is not right. Whoever acts wrongly not only gains nothing but does harm. Take a double-track railway: it must be level and straight without slant, and then the train can pass; if the rails are slanted and not true, the train cannot get through, and if forced along it will come to disaster. The principle of studying the Buddha Dharma is just the same.

Next, purity. To study the Buddha Dharma is to seek purity out of defilement. Take a bolt of white cloth: if it is heavily soiled, it must be washed before it can be clean. Let us ask ourselves: can we be without defilement? Not only are fame, profit, and respect a defilement of all kinds of greedy attachment; ignorance and affliction too are a defilement of thought after thought of toil. You should know that a single defilement is enough to harm body and mind, how much more many defilements! Therefore the practitioner must have the six senses undefiled. As the three karmas gradually dissolve, inner obstructions do not arise and outer dust does not defile; only thus can one be pure.

Next, mind. Śākyamuni Buddha sought teachers for five years, and all he met were not the right ones; when he attained the Way in the Snow Mountains, on what teacher did he rely? Did he not rely on the stillness and illumination of his own mind as his teacher? The Sixth Patriarch said: “When deluded, the teacher saves you; when awakened, you save yourself.” It is clear that only one who saves himself counts as an awakened person. If one does not rely on one's own mind, how can one save oneself? If the student of the Buddha Dharma does not rely on the teacher of his own mind's true emptiness and marklessness but seeks only outside the mind, saying today that this master's skill is high and tomorrow that that master's spiritual powers are great — what have the master's greatness and height to do with our own original portion? The more one seeks outwardly, the farther one is from the mind. To study the Buddha Dharma in this way is no different from driving south while the road goes north, and so one can never see the nature.

From what has been said above, one can see that Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and teacher are all not apart from one's own mind. If one departs from one's own mind, then whether one studies the exoteric or the esoteric, whether one discusses nature or marks, all is guest-dust and shadow. If one understands one's own mind, then the immeasurable Dharma gates are like family treasures hidden in one's own house, to be taken and used without ever running out; not only do exoteric and esoteric blend perfectly and nature and marks become non-dual, but even Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and teacher cannot be found. Therefore it is said that the markless refuge is precisely markless bodhi.

blocks.text: Fourth Sitting: The Mind-Ground Dharma

inline.s: Fellow students, we often pass over the four words “mind-ground Dharma” carelessly on the surface, not knowing that their meaning is of the greatest importance and the greatest breadth: if one can grasp them with care, one may awaken to the Way — what need is there for much seeking? Taken separately, “mind” is Buddha, “ground” is a figure for the measure of the mind, “dharma” means right, and “gate” means path. That is to say, if this mind can be like the ground, one enters the path of right awakening.

Our own mind is originally immeasurable and all-pervading; it can give rise to all dharmas, just as the great earth, possessing the virtue of breadth and depth, can give rise to all things — hence the figure. The reason the earth can give rise to all things is that it lets things take their course in season, doing nothing, utterly without knowing, still and unmoving. But living beings are deluded about the true and chase the false; seeing objects they give rise to thoughts, meeting things they are moved, and so they obscure their own numinous clarity and only increase their obstructions. The student of the Buddha Dharma, who uses the false to cultivate the true, should take the earth as his model. Yet mountains, rivers, and the great earth all arise from delusion and have their formation and destruction; why should we take delusion as our model? You should know that although the earth is delusion, its merit is immeasurable. The earth can produce all things, bear all things, and receive all things. Moreover, in producing all things it nourishes living beings, without selfish benefit for itself; in bearing all things it takes in great and small alike and holds clean and foul as one body, without the view of choosing or rejecting and discriminating; in receiving all things it lets people defile it, dig it, and hack it, still and unmoving, without thought of aversion, rejection, or hatred. This is why it is called the great earth. If our own measure of mind could be as great as the earth, could benefit others as the earth does, and were without the self-clinging of choosing and rejecting and hating, unmoved in all things, would it be hard to accord with the true suchness of our original mind? And what then would not be accomplished?

The Dharma we study is the mind-ground Dharma; day after day we speak of a mind-ground without wrong and of benefiting others without self — but after all, can our minds be as great as the earth? Can they nourish living beings? Can they take in and receive all, and let people defile and revile them without being moved? Not to speak of letting people revile us — I fear we cannot bear even one idle word. Not to speak of nourishing living beings — I fear that toward our own relatives we cannot escape selfishness and self-interest. And then we still speak of a mind-ground without wrong! One who studies the mind-ground Dharma must at every moment measure his own mind against the earth and see whether he can compare at all. As I see it, we cannot compare even to a single acre of ground, let alone to the great earth. Why? An acre of ground, through the four seasons of the year, can still bring forth many things to nourish living beings, and has the capacity to bear offense without retaliation. Let me ask, how does our own measure of mind compare with the productive capacity of that one acre? If you do not think and work on this point, you will never gain any benefit.

The earth can be great and can give rise, can bear and can receive, and it matches heaven in its virtue; therefore the ancients called the virtue of heaven and earth “great virtue.” Whatever measure of mind and merit is as great as the great earth is great virtue. A student of the Buddha Dharma who has already attained something is also called a person of great virtue. The Confucians say: “Therefore the greatly virtuous must obtain his place, must obtain his emolument, must obtain his name, must obtain his longevity.” One who studies the Buddha Dharma and becomes greatly virtuous regards place, emolument, name, and longevity as a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; only beginners who do not understand the Buddha Dharma mostly come seeking place, emolument, name, and longevity. But to obtain these, one must reach the stage of great virtue. And if one wishes to become greatly virtuous, one's measure of mind and merit must be as great as the great earth.

Fellow students! What is a bodhisattva who has ascended the grounds? Because his mind's measure and merit are truly as great as the great earth. As for bodhisattvas of the second and third grounds, their mind's measure and merit are as great as two or three earths. And those who go far beyond the tenth ground are called equal-awakening and wonderful-awakening. Think it over: is there in our mind's measure and merit so much as one earth? You should know that mind, Buddha, and living beings are three without difference. Our own mind-Buddha is originally complete with immeasurable merit, greater than the ten grounds; only because deluded thoughts never cease and we constantly cling to outer objects do we screen the true suchness of our own nature. It is like the light of sun and moon, which could shine everywhere, but because clouds and mist cover it, it does not appear. Once the clouds and mist disperse, the light returns at once. When a practitioner's single thought of the true mind suddenly transcends the ten grounds, it is the same. Therefore the bodhisattva Guang'e, putting down his butcher's knife, became a Buddha on the spot.

You should understand that the reason the great earth can accomplish such a great measure of merit is precisely that it is utterly unknowing and still and unmoving. Where we fall short is that we have many views and are easily moved. You should know that having many views and being easily moved all come from deluded thoughts that never cease. Deluded thought is fire: when our deluded thought stirs, it is like fire burning within the mind, and affliction arises. Therefore affliction is also called burning affliction, and it is the root of creating karma and suffering.

The three realms are mind only, and are also called the burning house. In the burning house there is originally a Dharma King; the student of the Buddha Dharma must seek the Dharma King within the burning house, and only then does he have true benefit. But ordinary beings take the illusory as real and abandon the real to chase the illusory. As it is said, when a film covers the eye, flowers in empty space fall in confusion; one sees only the flowers in empty space and not the Dharma King. They do not realize that the three realms are one mind, that when consciousness is turned it becomes wisdom, that when delusion is repented it becomes truth, and that truth is the Dharma King, seen without seeking. Ordinary beings do not awaken to this principle; their own minds are constantly burned by the flames of ignorance, and not only do they fail to see the Dharma King, but they are burned by these flames until the merit they originally possess is destroyed. As it is said, “When a single thought of hatred arises, the whole forest of merit is burned away.” We who study the Great Vehicle should know that all dharmas are like illusions, and that all dharmas are also true. In all matters, do not stir ignorance and do not give rise to affliction; recognize that bad is good and good is bad, and in all things neither grasp nor reject. Then not only can the fire not burn you, but this very fire turns into the light of wisdom, shining through boundlessly, one body with all the buddhas. Our own mind can originally govern itself, but because the power of concentration is insufficient it is constantly turned by karmic objects. Yet karma has no self-nature; if only we can empty out the mind of gain and loss, the mind of right and wrong, the mind of hatred, the mind of discrimination, and even the hundred and sixty kinds of successive mind and the eighty-four thousand minds of toil, then the wonderful luminous true mind will naturally appear before us, and we can share the virtue of heaven and earth.

The mind-ground Dharma, through the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, suddenly transcends and directly enters, making the ordinary a sage in this very life; it is also what bodhisattvas on the grounds practice. That you can practice this supreme Dharma means your conditions have ripened; I, Huiming, am doing no more than pointing the way. I hope you will do what is hard to do, endure what is hard to endure, give up what is hard to give up, and accomplish what is hard to accomplish, and strive to work on the mind-ground. If you meet it and do not meet it, see it and do not see it, and let this excellent opportunity pass, would it not be a pity? You should know that birth and death are a great matter, and impermanence is swift. We study the Buddha Dharma to resolve the question of birth and death; if we have some other purpose in mind, not only shall we gain no true benefit, but I fear we shall only increase our karmic obstructions. Let us not even speak of resolving birth and death: in this age of the Dharma's ending, with its kalpa of calamity, what affliction there is! Without a way to settle the mind and establish one's life, one easily gives rise to weariness with the world. But if one can rely on the mind-ground Dharma, practice the mind in earnest, learn the earth's measure and model the earth's virtue, then one will not only be cool and at ease, but can turn all things about — what calamity is there to fear? The purpose of the Buddha Dharma is originally to save the world and benefit living beings; put simply, it is to save people's minds. If a student of the Buddha Dharma wishes to save people's minds, he should first save his own mind. To save his own mind, he should work on his thoughts, repenting and removing all evil thoughts and increasing all good thoughts. Still more should he constantly examine whether his own mind is right, whether it is great, whether it can be as still and unmoved as the earth, whether it has merit as boundless as the earth's. Only thus does one truly practice the mind-ground Dharma. Let me give you four more lines of verse; ponder them carefully and they will naturally benefit you.
To learn the Buddha, seek not things outside; a heart of kindness holds all virtues inside.
When greed, hate, delusion, craving, and doubt are gone, unmoved by ignorance, the living Buddha lives on.

blocks.text: Fifth Sitting: The Dual Practice of Chan and Esoteric

inline.s: Fellow students, the mind-essence of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric cannot in principle be spoken; today I shall explain its meaning in skillful means. First a few words on the word Chan. Some take this word Chan to mean the dhyāna of the six pāramitās, and some take it to mean the prajñā-pāramitā of the six pāramitās. In fact the Chan of the Chan school encompasses the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, and means the transmission of mind by mind. Therefore Chan Master Yongjia said: “Suddenly awakened and clear — the Tathāgata's Chan, wherein the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices are perfected within the essence.” Some divide it into Tathāgata Chan and Patriarch Chan, not knowing that Patriarch Chan and Tathāgata Chan are the same mind-transmission. The Chan school began when Śākyamuni Buddha, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a flower before the multitude and transmitted it solely to Venerable Kāśyapa, who was named the first patriarch of the West. It was passed down singly through the generations, until the twenty-eighth patriarch, Great Master Bodhidharma, became the first patriarch of the East. Generation after generation they inherited it, mind secretly entrusting to mind — the so-called special transmission outside the teachings.

The true principle of the Buddha Dharma is beyond words and cut off from marks. The Chan school points directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha — a supreme Dharma gate. When the first patriarch came east, it was precisely for the one great matter of “this mind is Buddha.” But the realm of the Chan school is too high: those of dull faculties not only seldom awaken at a word, but mostly drift into mouth-Chan. For living beings in the age of the Dharma's ending mostly have deep and heavy karmic obstructions, and therefore the Esoteric is added. The Esoteric relies on the Buddha's power, Chan relies on one's own power; when Buddha-power and self-power become one, one can accord with capacities and enter deeply into the ultimate.

The mind-essence of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric has both a general and a particular meaning. What is the general meaning? First, the mind is explained. Chan is one's own mind, the Esoteric is the Buddha's mind. The Buddha's mind and one's own mind are originally one mind, all this wonderful, luminous, perfect-awakening mind. Next, the essence is explained. Whatever is expressed in words is the teachings; what does not rely on words is the essence. The Chan school does not rely on words and points directly at the human mind, and so it is called the essence. The Esoteric Dharma, though it has mantra texts, follows only their sound and does not comprehend their meaning; it is spoken yet not spoken, words yet no words, and so it too is called the essence. Therefore the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is called the mind-essence. What is the particular meaning? Chan and Esoteric each have two.

First, Chan is explained. (1) In accord with the patriarch's intent: Chan is the mind-Dharma transmitted by Patriarch Bodhidharma, which does not rely on written or spoken words but transmits mind by mind; hence it is called the mind-essence. (2) In accord with the Buddha's intent: Śākyamuni Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet said himself that he had not spoken a single word; and at the assembly on Vulture Peak he transmitted the mind to Venerable Kāśyapa, entrusting him, saying: “I have the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma, the wonderful mind of nirvāṇa, the mark of reality which is markless; I entrust it to you, that it not be cut off.” This treasury of the eye of the true Dharma is the mysterious mind of the mark of reality, which is markless; hence it is called the mind-essence.

Next, the Esoteric is explained. (1) General explanation. The Mahāvairocana Sutra says: “What is bodhi? It is knowing one's own mind as it truly is.” Hence it is called the mind-essence. Moreover the esoteric mantras are also called true words; in Sanskrit they are called dhāraṇī, which means total retention. All esoteric mantras are the subtle original minds of the buddhas and bodhisattvas, secret and hard to know, to be recited but not to be spoken of; hence it is called the mind-essence. (2) Particular explanation. There are eighty-four thousand kinds of esoteric mantra; this six-syllable great bright mantra was spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and is the subtle original mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, that is, the wonderful mind of all the buddhas, and also the one mind of living beings. To transmit the six-syllable great bright mantra is to transmit mind by mind; hence it is called the mind-essence.

The Chan school's special transmission outside the teachings does not rely on the scriptures, does not establish gradual stages, and holds that this very mind is Buddha — the so-called transmission of mind by mind. The ancient worthies taught people mostly amid joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, striking from the side and tapping askew, openly opening and secretly prompting, with great capacity and great function, all to bring the student to awaken at once to his own mind and step straight into the Tathāgata's treasure house; hence it is called the supreme vehicle. But its failing is that it easily leads students to stop at a shallow awakening and no longer engage in practice, or to take quiescence as the practice and not know how to rise up and function. The Esoteric school has heavy ritual and advances step by step, from small to great, omitting no dharma and overstepping no dharma; first one practices the preliminaries, and then one is given the true word of the chosen deity. Then from recitation one goes on to visualization, and gradually to the markless prajñā. By self-power and other-power together, one enters the three mysteries as one thusness, and the ordinary becomes a sage. But its failing is that it easily leads students to delight in spiritual powers and to fall into Mara's realm. Moreover the making of ritual implements, the adornment of the sanctuary, the offerings to the guru, and so on, cannot be managed by anyone who is not wealthy and also at leisure. Only the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric takes from Chan the teaching that one's own mind is Buddha and that the mark of reality is markless, to save the Esoteric from the danger of clinging to marks and falling into Mara; and takes from the Esoteric its single-minded emphasis on practice in actual fact and its use of inconceivable power to transform living beings, to remedy the Chan school's shallow awakening that stops short, its marklessness and non-attainment, and its biased refusal to rise up and save living beings. Therefore in the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric one does not cling one-sidedly to the ritual altar, nor must one master gradual stages; so long as one's faculties correspond and conditions have ripened, rich or poor, old or young, all may practice. Knowing on the one hand that in the Chan school mind itself is Buddha, yet not abandoning practice in actual fact, and knowing on the other hand that in the Esoteric Dharma, by the Buddha's empowering grace, there is something mysterious beyond the mind, yet not clinging to mysterious marks — thus one can certainly attain accomplishment in this very body. In the age of the Dharma's ending, this is the Dharma gate that accords with capacities and gathers all in.

Though the Esoteric Dharma has spiritual powers, you should know that these powers arise from the subtle original mind and from the inconceivable, and are still illusion and delusion; students must on no account crave and cling to them. Any esoteric practitioner who delights in speaking of spiritual powers not only confuses what people see and hear, but easily falls into Mara. The ancient worthies said: “Spiritual powers and healing are the least of a sage's concerns.” You should know that the function of the Esoteric Dharma is to make the ordinary a sage in this very life; it cannot be spoken of — how should it lie in spiritual powers and healing? Nowadays the Eastern Esoteric and the Tibetan Esoteric are in vogue throughout the country, which is truly an excellent condition for the Buddha Dharma. But students mostly crave much and seek to gain; having received one practice, before they have even gained a response they want a second. Today a vajra guru comes and they go to take refuge; tomorrow an ācārya comes and they go to take refuge, not knowing where their study must reach to be ultimate. You should know that in practicing the Esoteric one must penetrate deeply through one gate, have faith in teacher and Dharma, and above all be unchanging to the end; only then can one reach the inconceivable realm.

All the Dharma gates the Buddha taught ultimately return to one mind. Because living beings cling to marks, and out of fear that they would cling to words, he made the special transmission outside the teachings, beyond words and cut off from marks, to reveal the essence that mind itself is Buddha; and he especially taught the Esoteric Dharma to show the function of the subtle original mind of the buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Tathāgata was so compassionate, using all kinds of skillful means to reveal the essentials of the mind, yet living beings take the exoteric as not the esoteric and the esoteric as not the exoteric, and so lose the pearl in their own robe — truly to be pitied. I, Huiming, now propagate the mind-essence of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric: taking Chan as the essence and the Esoteric as the function, using Chan to embrace the Esoteric and the Esoteric to protect Chan — that is, using mind to embrace mind and using mind to protect mind. You should know that Chan and Esoteric, though two in name, are in fact one. Only, of the two schools, one gives weight to awakening and the other to practice; in the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric one should give equal weight to practice and awakening. Do not think that Chan is sudden awakening and has no need of practice in actual fact; you should know that though the principle is suddenly awakened, practice is valued for being gradual. Why? When the wind has ceased the waves are not yet calm; when the filth is removed the stench remains — the habits of many lives and many ages must be practiced away before they are purified. It is like gold in the ore: its nature is gold, but unless it is mined, washed, and smelted it cannot become pure gold. The six-syllable great bright mantra has merit immeasurable and boundless; if only one practices it with utmost sincerity and single-mindedness, with the mind's thought not two, it will naturally have inconceivable power to dissolve fundamental karmic obstructions and accomplish buddhahood in this very body. If one cannot penetrate deeply through one gate, if one's mind of discrimination is heavy, or if one does not arouse a mind of great compassion, then one will not correspond. You should know that in the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric one takes saving the world and delivering living beings as one's vow, takes the Buddha's mind as one's own mind, and holds that the chosen deity is myself and I am the chosen deity. If one can arouse such a great mind, one will naturally be mind sealing mind with all the buddhas and bodhisattvas and with the chosen deity. And since mind, Buddha, and living beings are three without difference, it is called the mind-essence.

blocks.text: Sixth Sitting: The Mind-Essence Cures the Mind's Illness

inline.s: Fellow students, the weather has been abnormal lately and many have caught cold. You should know that our illnesses go beyond this; let me say a little about the sources of illness and their treatment, as follows.

Illness is of two kinds, formless and formed. Formless illness is greed, hatred, delusion, craving, and all afflictions. Formed illness is external attack and internal injury, and all disharmony of the four elements. Formless illness is the illness of the mind; formed illness is the illness of the body. Bodily illness arises from mental illness: if the mind is without illness, the body is not ill either. But this mind is originally pure, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure — how can it be ill? Only because of the very first thought of deluded movement is there this body; and having a body is itself illness. Furthermore, because feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness stubbornly grasp a self, deluded thoughts and clinging arise, and from greed, hatred, delusion, and craving come the eighty-four thousand afflictions, which give rise to mental illness. From this mental illness come all kinds of bodily illness. So birth, aging, sickness, and death turn with karma, and there is no time when we are not in suffering. Since we know that bodily illness has its source in mental illness, and mental illness has its source in the movement of thought, the source of illness is clear, and we should apply the remedy to the disease. What is the remedy? The dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is the agada medicine that cures the root and clears the source. This medicine was transmitted by Śākyamuni Buddha as the wonderful cure for living beings' suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death; it cures all illnesses of body and mind alike, and therefore the Tathāgata is also called the Great King of Physicians.

The student of the Buddha Dharma knows the illness and seeks the medicine, and so can escape suffering. But living beings in their dream, though ill, do not know they are ill; they mistake suffering for medicine, not knowing that the boundless sea of karma is immeasurable, and that rich and poor, wise and foolish, none can escape the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death. So there is suffering in having, and suffering in not having. Those who have, merely had more good causes in past kalpas; but once the good causes are exhausted, evil fruit follows: at the least they are reborn as humans, foolish and disabled; at the worst they fall into the three evil paths and sink for long kalpas. These matters of cause and effect and the turning of rebirth are recorded in ancient books or handed down in anecdotes — by no means false or fantastic. It is a pity that people of the world do not awaken, and add illness to illness — truly pitiable. In recent times natural and man-made calamities have come one after another; not only is there the misery of birth, aging, and sickness, but the dead too are counted in thousands and tens of thousands. Such shared karma is all brought about by the common mental illness of living beings. And the common mental illness is in turn induced by each person's single thought of deluded movement. For when one's own mind is impure, the minds of others become impure, and drawing one another on, they form shared karma. If one awakens to the truth that all is illusion and keeps thought after thought pure, then at once body and mind are light and at ease. If one's own mental illness diminishes, the common mental illness diminishes too. Why? Because when one's own mind is pure, the minds of others are pure. If one will not let go, but clings to everything, then everything is enough to make oneself ill and to make others ill. As the proverb says, “The illness of the mind has no medicine.” Therefore our Buddha in his compassion broadly taught eighty-four thousand Dharma gates to cure the eighty-four thousand illnesses of toil of living beings. What you are now studying, the mind-essence of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, is precisely the mind-medicine that can cut off the source of illness. If only you are willing to take the medicine, the mind's illness can certainly be cured. When the mind's illness is cured, not only is bodily illness cured too, but all illness is cured; what need then to seek further among the eighty-four thousand kinds of Dharma medicine? Apart from the time of sitting meditation, when you can purify the mind a little, how many thoughts do you have each day? Every thought is an illness — how much illness is that! You should know that a single illness can keep a person from rising; how much more many illnesses! Recently some of you have caught cold: at first it was only a small illness, but if it is not treated early, or the wrong medicine is taken, it may turn into a grave illness and even cause death. In the same way, a single wrong thought seems to ordinary feeling to be of no weight, but you do not realize that thought follows thought without cease, until affliction is boundless and illness is added to illness. You should know that birth and death are a great matter, and how long is a human life? I hope you will rouse yourselves, and quickly practice the mind according to the Dharma to cure the mind's illness. Here is a verse that can cure illnesses both formed and formless.
Your own sickness your own mind knows; the body's sickness the mind's medicine cures.
When the mind is right the body is pure; when the mind is born, sickness is sure.

Fellow students, though this verse is but four plain lines, if you can ponder it carefully, or take it as a true word and recite it, it will surely have wonderful effect. You should know that the ordinary method of the Chan school is to investigate a huatou, a word-head; there are live huatous and dead huatous, given according to the depth of the student's capacity. This verse may be taken as a live huatou to investigate; investigated long, one will surely awaken to something. Do not slight it because it is plain.

When we are ill, because we do not know the source of the illness we use medicines at random, and in the end they are of no effect. If we never know it ourselves, then as illness deepens and karma grows heavy we fall into the three evil paths, and it is even harder to know. To know what? To know that illness is born of karma, karma is born of affliction, and affliction is born of ignorance. When ignorance stirs, mental illness becomes bodily illness; hence, “Your own sickness your own mind knows.” The root illness cannot be cured by medicine, nor can relying solely on the Buddha's power easily bring results. For illness arises from the mind and must be cured by the mind; hence, “The body's sickness the mind's medicine cures.” What is mind-medicine? A right mind is the medicine — that is, right knowledge, right view, and right thought. If the mind has something it resents, something it fears, something it delights in, something it worries over, these are all affliction, and none of them is right. When the mind is not right, it moves deludedly with circumstances, gives rise to confusion and creates karma, and so bodily illness forms. If the mind can be right, then the mind is at peace and the body at ease, and the body is pure of itself. What is called cultivating the person lies in making the mind right — this is the principle that when the mind is right the body is pure. Hence, “When the mind is right the body is pure.” The essence of the mind is originally empty, still, and numinously clear; once it moves, obstruction arises. Not only are evil thoughts illness — every thought is illness; as it is said, every thought is wrong. This is speaking one level deeper. Hence, “When the mind is born, sickness is born.”

There are many ways to explain these four lines, and to explain them too clearly is rather unhelpful. For the Chan huatou, like the true word of the Esoteric Dharma, has the effect of breaking views and opinions; investigated and recited long, one will naturally awaken to the Way. Now calamity is not yet over, and living beings are all in illness. Since your conditions have ripened and you have come to study this supreme mind-ground Dharma, and you now know both the source of illness and the medicine that cures it, I hope you will follow this prescription, practice according to the Dharma, and awaken and practice at once. What is practice? Practicing all good dharmas. All good dharmas means benefiting others; only in benefiting others is there merit. With merit one can be right, can be pure; and being pure, one is without illness. If one does not do the work of benefiting others but merely recites mantras and sits in meditation, though there is merit, the benefit is not great. If the aspiration is genuine and karma is gradually dissolved, bodily and mental illness may also be reduced. The mind-essence of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is meant not only to cure one's own mental illness but, more, to cure the mental illness of living beings. Why? Because we should base ourselves on the vow that until all living beings are saved we will not be saved, and look on the illness of living beings as our own. Therefore we should be great, brave, and fearless, with all compassion, and propagate the mind-ground Dharma to cure the mental illness of living beings everywhere. If living beings are without illness, my illness too is gone — only this is the true purport of the mind-essence's cure of mental illness.

blocks.text: Seventh Sitting: False Practice and True Practice

inline.s: Fellow students, in the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric there is a distinction between false practice and true practice. And within true practice, resolve and perseverance are each hard to keep. You should know that it is easy to study the Buddha Dharma but hard to practice; easy to practice falsely but hard to practice truly; easy to resolve but hard to persevere. Any student of the Buddha Dharma who turns back in regret midway does so because he has not resolved on true practice, or has resolved but lacks perseverance. If one vows to practice truly, has resolve, and can persevere, one will certainly not turn back. Let me now divide these into four meanings and explain them briefly.

What is false practice? Our physical body is fundamentally false; to seek the true, therefore, there is practice, and so it is called using the false to cultivate the true. Only by giving up the false can one gain the true. If one clings to marks everywhere on the false self and does not work on the true self, this is called false practice. All Dharma gates originate in the mind; the mind is the true self, and to seek outside the mind is not to correspond — this too is called false practice. The mind-ground Dharma teaches people to sit in meditation, which is cultivating the mind; it teaches people to recite mantras, which is gathering in the mind. But if, when on the seat, the body sits while the mind does not sit; or when reciting, the mouth recites while the mind does not recite — this too is called false practice. In the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, a mind-ground without wrong is the root of the precepts, and benefiting others without self is right practice; one who truly practices this is walking the bodhisattva path. If one only knows sitting in meditation and seeks solely for one's own liberation, and even becomes arrogant, boastful, and jealous, giving rise to affliction at every turn, then one does not correspond with this method — this too is false practice.

What is true practice? At all times, in all places, toward all things, not clinging to marks and not apart from marks. When on the seat, body and mind both sit; when reciting, mind and mouth recite together, and body and mind become one piece. And with the purport of benefiting others without self, one arouses a mind of great compassion, rises up in the practice of spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings, and with bitter words and a kind heart urges people to do no evil and to practice all good. Still more must one be not two in mind and deed, unchanging to the end — this is true practice. Such true practice is not a hard matter; the reason it cannot be carried out is only that one has not made the resolve, and is easily turned by outer circumstances.

What is resolve? It means putting everything down, penetrating deeply through one gate, and advancing bravely and diligently. The root of the Buddha Dharma is to escape birth and death and to save all living beings — how great a matter, how difficult! Without making a resolve, how could it be attained by luck? Śākyamuni Buddha, with the honor of a crown prince, in the prime of his youth, saw the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death and could awaken to the false and turn to the true, tossing aside the throne like a worn sandal, seeking teachers everywhere for five years, and practicing austerities in the Snow Mountains for six years — what was his resolve like? The Second Patriarch Huike, when he went to visit the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, stood in the snow all night, and the First Patriarch, facing the wall, paid him no heed but rebuked him: “The supreme wonderful Way of the buddhas is attained by diligent effort through vast kalpas, doing what is hard to do and enduring what is hard to endure; even so it is not yet reached — how can you seek the great Dharma for such slight toil and small effect?” Hearing this instruction, the Second Patriarch cut off his arm with a knife — what was his resolve like? Think it over. The First Patriarch had come east precisely to transmit the Dharma to the Second Patriarch, crossing the sea for three years and facing the wall for nine. When the Second Patriarch came a thousand miles to visit him, why did he at first pay no heed and even rebuke him, and only when he saw the severed arm as a token of his purpose allow him to enter? This was to test whether he had resolve. In practicing this Dharma gate, you should take the resolve of our Buddha and our Patriarch as your resolve.
