Moreover, in this life we study the Buddha Dharma and, through conditions, have come to hear the supreme mind-ground Dharma; we need not leave home to become monks, nor endure the Snow Mountains and the cutting off of an arm. If we still do not make a resolve, are we not willingly casting ourselves away?

What is perseverance? It means being unchanging to the end and never turning back through a hundred setbacks. A student of the Buddha Dharma has made his resolve and vowed to advance diligently, yet after no long time his spirit scatters, or meeting adverse circumstances his doubts multiply, and so he changes. Why is this? The fault lies in lacking perseverance; without perseverance nothing is accomplished, let alone studying the Buddha Dharma! Though one may have a moment's resolve, it is the same as having none. You should know that in studying the Buddha Dharma and accomplishing the Way, unless one passes through nine hardships and nine perils one cannot reach the ultimate. It is like rowing a boat against the current: not to advance is to fall back, and one moment of slackness undoes all previous work. Therefore after resolving on true practice one must be wholly without interruption and press straight ahead; though space itself may be destroyed, the vow-power does not shift, and naturally the defilement is purified, the light appears, the water clears, and the moon is revealed. But where do perseverance and its absence come from? They lie in whether the aspiration is of utmost sincerity or not. Whoever resolves but lacks perseverance acts from a single impulse, not from utmost sincerity. If the aspiration comes from utmost sincerity, then one has a settled view and will never stop halfway. As it is said, utmost sincerity never ceases; not ceasing, it endures; enduring, one has perseverance; and with perseverance one can naturally see the nature. Those who cannot resolve and persevere are obstructed by karmic force from beginningless time; therefore they should devoutly recite the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra as preliminaries. These two sutras are both the prajñā of the mark of reality, and their response is extraordinary: not only can they dissolve offenses from beginningless past lives, but they can increase blessing and wisdom. If one recites them with perseverance, one may understand the mind and see the nature.

Chan is the mind-transmission of all the buddhas, the Esoteric is the mind-seal of all the buddhas; the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is truly the supreme Dharma gate, hard to meet and hard to encounter. One must possess supreme resolve and the utmost sincerity of vow and practice to enter deeply. Only with the courage to pour out wealth and life and with a spirit of firmness and hardship unsurpassed is there hope of understanding the mind and seeing the nature. For great giving brings great gain, and without giving there is no gain. In this age of the Dharma's ending, though bodhisattvas come by vow, they too are subject to the delusion of the intervening life; if they do not quickly awaken, I fear they will fall along with living beings — is that not dangerous? Among you there are indeed many who have aroused the aspiration and are diligent, but there are also inevitably some who interrupt and lack perseverance, advancing and retreating by turns, and in the end only harming themselves. Formerly, fearing that the bhikṣus would be indolent and without perseverance, the Buddha had a method of warning: he taught the bhikṣus, when weariness and indolence arose, to rub their own heads. Rubbing the head, one feels that one has shaved one's hair and become a monk for the sake of escaping birth and death. Having thought of escaping birth and death, then though there be a thousand hardships and ten thousand bitter toils, though body be ground to powder and bones shattered, one does not shrink. Naturally the mind of diligence arises and the mind of weariness recedes. You who practice at home cannot rub your heads to warn yourselves, but you may recall your elders and old friends, old or young, who have died, many of them, and silently picture the pain of their deathbed; at the same time you awaken to the fact that before long your own body will be the same. Then you will naturally be able to resolve, and naturally rise up in perseverance. Hence it is said, “Buddha means awakened; awakened, one is Buddha.” Awakened to what? Awakened that all worldly dharmas are illusory, awakened that birth, aging, sickness, and death are fearful, awakened that one's own manifold afflictions and sufferings are in the end unavoidable, and that all the success and failure, rise and fall of worldly dharmas are a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow — all of them objects that urge us to awakening. If one can constantly hold up this mirror, one can awaken anywhere; why fear that one cannot persevere?

Fellow students, the Chan school is now in a time of turning the light back to shine within, and the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric also has its season: a flower blooms but once, the moon is hard to round again; do not miss this life's opportunity. The merit of the six-syllable great bright mantra is immeasurable and is recorded in full in the Sutra of the Great, Precious, Adorned King of the Great Vehicle; if you can resolve on true practice and remain unchanging, you will surely have inconceivable benefit. Among you, many have already gained inconceivable responses. You should know that such responses are the empowering grace of the buddhas. It is like aged parents whose only son suddenly runs away and is long without news; when at last he comes home from afar, how could they not leap with joy and cherish him? Yet the reason these parents cherish the son who ran away and returned is not merely that they have someone to rely on in their old age; it is that they rejoice that someone will inherit the family estate and continue the line. The compassion and care of the buddhas and bodhisattvas for those who practice truly is just the same. But one who practices truly should shoulder the Tathāgata's family estate, propagate the true Dharma, and save living beings. Yet in saving living beings the first thing is merit: if one's own merit is insufficient, one cannot even save one's own family — how can one save others? Hence the Confucians say: “There is no one who, unable to teach his own household, can teach others.” What is merit? A mind-ground without wrong is merit; benefiting others without self is virtue. A right mind is merit; right action is virtue. The six pāramitās and ten thousand practices are great merit. What the First Patriarch Bodhidharma called pure wisdom, perfect and wonderful, its essence empty and still of itself, is true merit. Such merit is in truth not easy. But if we can practice truly, having both resolve and perseverance, great, brave, and fearless, compassionate and without self, seeing all living beings as future buddhas, as living buddhas now, or as parents from past kalpas — then, as it is said, if I wish for benevolence, benevolence is at hand; what difficulty is there?

blocks.text: Eighth Sitting: Mind-Thoughts and the Critical Junctures

inline.s: Fellow students, the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is simple and easy in method, but mind-thoughts and the critical junctures are of the greatest importance. If one does not work on mind-thoughts, one is seeking the Dharma outside the mind; if one does not understand the critical junctures, one wanders without aim. Not knowing the subtle marks of mind-thoughts, one not only cannot advance diligently but may go astray midway. Why? The Chan school sees the nature and becomes Buddha, the Esoteric makes the ordinary a sage — both are supreme Dharma gates; without correspondence in mind-thoughts and clarity about the critical junctures, how can one enter deeply? I shall now say a little about the mind-thoughts and critical junctures of this method, and I hope you will take note.

The Esoteric Dharma appears in the world for an inconceivable great matter. It is to cause living beings in the three evil paths to be born in the three good paths, and living beings in the three good paths to transcend the three realms and quickly accomplish the Buddha Way. One who practices the Esoteric receives the empowerment of the three mysteries, and can cause the fierce fires of hell to become a seven-jeweled lotus pond, and boundless burning affliction to be cool at once. With seven grains of rice one can satisfy all the hungry ghosts of the Dharma realm and free them from suffering to gain happiness. This is our Buddha's wonderful way of transforming living beings and saving the world — how could it be a mere minor art of healing illness and praying for rain, having nothing to do with the life of wisdom? Such inconceivable merit cannot be attained without correspondence in mind-thoughts and great virtue. Therefore the Esoteric school takes the bodhi mind as cause and great compassion as root. The root of the Chan school is that one's own mind is Buddha. What is Buddha? To be free of marks is Buddha. The Sixth Patriarch said: “The Dharma gate of the Chan school takes no-thought as its essence and no-mark as its substance. No-thought and no-mark are bodhi. When bodhi rises up and functions, that is compassion.” From this, both Chan and Esoteric take the bodhi mind as cause and great compassion as root. The bodhi mind is the mind of great compassion. In the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric one must possess such mind-thoughts to correspond.

Three mysteries: the mystery of body, the mystery of speech, and the mystery of mind. Speaking of the Buddha realm, Mahāvairocana Tathāgata is a body pervading the Dharma realm, and so the substance and marks of the Dharma realm are his body-mystery; all sounds are his speech-mystery; and the all-pervading element of consciousness is his mind-mystery. Speaking of living beings, forming hand seals is the body-mystery, reciting true words is the speech-mystery, and the mind contemplating the marks of the chosen deity is the mind-mystery. Three-mystery empowerment: the empowerment of the Buddha's three mysteries. When living beings practice the three mysteries, their three karmas of body, speech, and mind receive the empowerment of the Buddha's three mysteries; Buddha and living being correspond in the three mysteries and blend without interval, and then inconceivable power is produced, and this body can become Buddha. At this time a power beyond the human appears; this correspondence and the response obtained are called empowerment.

Whoever practices the Esoteric Dharma relies entirely on the empowering grace of the Buddha's power. To obtain the Buddha's empowering grace, one must first arouse the bodhi mind, see all things as one body, the six paths as sharing one life, pity the suffering of birth and death of self and others, and vow to save all living beings. Then practice diligently according to the Dharma, allowing not a single moment's thought to go against compassion; when sincerity reaches its height, it naturally moves the buddhas and devas. Then the Buddha's power empowering one person is empowering all, and how could there be no response and correspondence? If one knows only self-benefit and clings to marks in vain seeking, correspondence is exceedingly hard. The Chan school's seeing the nature and becoming Buddha requires using prajñā wisdom to break all marks of delusion and using a mind of compassion and equality to save all, and then bodhi is perfected. If one only sits in empty stillness and investigates dryly, without arousing the mind of compassion, how can one correspond with the Buddha of one's own mind? Yet the Buddha of self and the Buddha of others are fundamentally not two; correspondence lies only in mind-thoughts. But to speak of it is not hard, to practice it is hard — why is this? Because the karmic habits of past lives are unavoidable for everyone, and at the time of practice they become obstructions. The Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sutra says briefly: Bodhisattvas at the causal stage have five kinds of covering obstruction. First, the obstruction of affliction: that is, fundamental affliction, and on down to the eighty-four thousand afflictions of upper, middle, and lower grades, which cover the pure mind. Second, the obstruction of karma: that is, the grave offenses committed in past and present, which, not yet removed, prevent entry into the Way. Third, the obstruction of birth: because of past karma one is afflicted by illness or Mara, receives a body without leisure, and cannot advance diligently. Fourth, the obstruction of Dharma: that is, having had conditions obstructing the Dharma in past kalpas, in this life one does not hear the true Dharma, or cannot penetrate deeply through one gate. Fifth, the obstruction of the known: that is, having already met a good teacher, one's various views and opinions do not accord with his, hindering the cultivation of prajñā. Even bodhisattvas at the causal stage have such covering obstructions — how much more those below them! Without a vast and genuine mind and brave repentance, how can all covering obstructions be removed? Therefore the mind-thought of bodhi and compassion is the root of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric.

Bodhi is markless, and nothing can be attained. If the student clings to marks everywhere and seeks to attain everywhere, his mind-thoughts cannot correspond with markless bodhi. One who seeks blessings: when the reward is exhausted he falls again, and his toil has been in vain. One who seeks recovery from illness: birth, aging, sickness, and death cannot in the end be escaped. Such clinging to marks and vain seeking may not even gain what is sought — how much less, when gain entails loss! Gain and loss disturb the mind, doubt and wavering shake the faith, and there is none who does not change and turn back in regret. Only by taking marklessness as the root and seeing all that has marks as delusion can gain and loss fail to move the mind, hardships fail to dishearten the will, and danger fail to break the spirit. Naturally one is great, brave, and fearless, pressing straight ahead with utmost sincerity that is not two. One can then share the virtue of heaven and earth and the brightness of sun and moon, and gain without seeking. There is no mark of Dharma, and no non-mark of Dharma. And even to self and other being not two, embracing all equally, seeing the suffering and misery of living beings as no different from what one endures oneself, saving all living beings yet without the mind-thought of saving or being saved — this is the markless bodhi that is in marks and yet apart from marks.

Though among those who practice the Esoteric Dharma there are some who for a time develop spiritual powers, the matter of spiritual powers must absolutely not be spoken of or revealed; otherwise one will certainly invite Mara's obstruction. Why? To reveal them deliberately is to cling to marks and to seek. To cling to marks and seek is to have an impure mind. To have an impure mind is to enter Mara's realm oneself. One who enters Mara's realm himself not only traps himself by his spiritual powers, but will surely cause those who see and hear to cast away their own minds and enter Mara's net with him. That is to drive the Buddha's disciples to become Mara's retinue — a crime great and heinous, deserving of the hells. In the Śūraṅgama Sutra's fifty kinds of skandha-Mara, there is a Mara of joy for joy and a Mara of anger for anger; and even clinging to emptiness or to purity brings the Mara of emptiness and the Mara of purity — how dangerous! Therefore the Esoteric Dharma is not transmitted to those unfit for it. One who studies the Esoteric must receive transmission from a greatly virtuous ācārya, and at the time of practice must have the ācārya's protection. The Eastern and Tibetan Esoteric schools also have all kinds of ritual implements and adorned sanctuaries, and even the business of purifying the altar must be handled by oneself — in part to follow the esoteric ritual and arouse devotion, and in part to gather in the mind-thoughts and avoid clinging to outer objects. You should know that spiritual powers are complete in one's own nature and are not sought from outside. If only one possesses mind-thoughts of great compassion, is firm and unsurpassed in hardship, and never turns back through a hundred setbacks, then when sincerity moves the other, one will naturally meet a great good teacher to enlighten one. When the water clears and the moon appears, one realizes that the ten thousand dharmas are not apart from one's own mind. But one who does not arouse a great mind, who imitates the pattern in the gourd and clings to marks in seeking, even if he gains a little response, it is still a mystery outside the mind; and if he takes it as a saintly understanding, he falls into Mara's path. As for the responses each of you has in your practice, you should know that they all come about because you have aroused the aspiration, and so the Buddha's power empowers you to strengthen your faith and aid your diligence. If you do not take such responses as saintly understanding, they are simply states. Therefore in my recorded sayings it is said: the states seen in sitting should not be met with mark-clinging and thought-arising; not delighting and not fearing, neither grasping nor rejecting, is the right principle. Here is a verse.
Cling to marks, and Mara takes the mind; leave marks behind, and ease you find.
All things seen with an equal eye — nothing grasped and nothing cast by.

The dual practice of Chan and Esoteric is a Dharma gate of skillful means. It opens the door and sees the mountain, does not enter by gradual stages, does not give weight to the marks of practice, and does not lean to one side in discussing theory; the point of entry is to work on mind-thoughts. If the mind-thoughts are pure, bodhi arises, and one transcends the ordinary and enters the sage. If the mind-thoughts are not pure, one gives rise to confusion and creates karma, and that is an ordinary being. Only the sage, if he is without mindfulness, becomes mad; only the mad, if he can master mindfulness, becomes a sage. So the difference between ordinary being and sage lies in mind-thoughts alone. But within this there are critical junctures and stages that must not go unknown. The Chan school's investigating a huatou and the Esoteric's reciting true words differ as self-power and Buddha-power, yet self and other are not two: both are beyond speech, and both use this to lock out all deluded thoughts. The function of the true word is even more inconceivable, and therefore this method recites only the six-syllable true word (Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ) and does not use a huatou. With this true word one destroys all seeds of deluded thought. When views and opinions no longer arise and deluded thoughts are purified, the true mind naturally appears before one, and the Buddha of self and the Buddha of others correspond as one body.

As for the critical junctures: Chan investigation is generally divided into three gates — the first gate, the heavy gate, and the firm gate — and this method also has three gates. What is the first gate? When the student recites the true word until ten thousand thoughts return to one and no second thought arises, this is called passing the first gate. But this is pressing grass down with a stone, and is not yet ultimate. What is the second gate? When the true word is recited to the point of reciting without reciting and not reciting while reciting, and who it is that recites even oneself does not know — when at the same time it seems as though two people are reciting together — this is called samādhi appearing before one, and also called passing the second gate. What is the third gate? When the true word is recited to the point where true, false, and dharma are all three unknown, and one enters deeply into samādhi and attains concentration that is free of reciting, with nothing whatsoever, and realizes the mark of reality, complete with all things — this is called passing the third gate. Of those who have investigated Chan from of old, some have passed the first and second gates, but passing the third gate is very hard. These critical junctures matter greatly; if they are not clear, one cannot tell the shallow from the deep, and easily risks calling what is not attained an attainment and what is not realized a realization. As for those who practice Chan, a single phrase of “the Buddha of one's own mind” often becomes mouth-Chan — as it is said, nine out of ten take the wrong road; and those who practice the Esoteric vie in marvels and display the extraordinary, seeking mark upon mark — none of it is ultimate.

The mind-thoughts and critical junctures of the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, summed up, are no more than three: first, breaking the false; second, revealing the true; third, the non-duality of true and false. The empowerment of the three mysteries is breaking the false. Reciting the true word to the point of attaining nothing whatsoever is revealing the true. Mind is Buddha and Buddha is mind — that is the non-duality of true and false. One who practices both Chan and Esoteric, basing himself on these three and working on mind-thoughts, will pass through the critical junctures and naturally break the false and reveal the true, and even reach the non-duality of true and false.

blocks.text: Ninth Sitting: Affliction and Bodhi

inline.s: Fellow students, what is affliction-bodhi? Affliction and bodhi do not go outside one mind. The matter of affliction is indeed a stage that every practitioner must pass through in realizing bodhi; I shall say a little about it now. Affliction-bodhi contains two meanings: first, the meaning of a lotus born in fire; second, the meaning of turning consciousness into wisdom.

What is the meaning of a lotus born in fire? Fire is a figure for affliction, the lotus a figure for bodhi. Affliction is suffering, bodhi is joy. If a student of the Buddha Dharma wishes to pass from suffering to joy, he must bring forth a red lotus from within the burning house of affliction — only that is ultimate. Why? Fire has the power to destroy: things that are not real, once touched by its flame, all dissolve along with it. It also has the power to temper: substances that are firm and true, receiving its smelting, become a body of diamond that cannot be destroyed, and not only are they not broken by anything, but they can break everything. The practitioner must be ground and smelted within the burning house of affliction. Taking affliction as a good condition that spurs the arousal of the aspiration, and hardship as the furnace that tempers body and mind — only by working in this way does one become a vessel of the Dharma. Without the grinding of affliction, one not only finds it hard to arouse a great mind, but even if one has a small attainment, as soon as circumstances press upon one, one is turned by them. So it was with the Second Patriarch standing in the snow and cutting off his arm, the Sixth Patriarch selling firewood and pounding rice, and Hanshan Deqing going to prison for the Dharma; and even those who begged for alms and took menial service, who burned their fingers or their bodies, or who gave their bodies to feed a tiger — of such examples there is no end, and not one of them came by it without being ground and tempered amid difficulties and dangers. As it is said, if you do not enter the tiger's den, how can you get the tiger's cub? Hence, “The Way is sought amid suffering.” Moreover, to study the Buddha Dharma is to go against the current and return to the source; if one does not go against the current, how can one return to the source? The way of going against the current is not only so in the Buddha Dharma — in every matter and every thing it is the same. If a sword is not ground, it is not sharp; if jade is not cut, it does not become a vessel; if heaven had no autumn's killing and winter's storing, how could it accomplish the glory of spring's birth and summer's growth? If a person had no firm and unsurpassed going against the current, how could he create works that save the world and benefit people? Had Shun not had the adversity of a foolish father, a wicked mother, and an arrogant brother, how could he have made the name of his great filial piety? Had Yu not had the adversity of the great flood and his father's execution, how could he have made the achievement of controlling the waters? From this one may know that the fire of affliction is the cause of bodhi; this is the meaning of a lotus born in fire.

What is the meaning of turning consciousness into wisdom? Clinging to marks and discriminating is consciousness; being in marks yet apart from marks is wisdom. Consciousness is affliction, wisdom is bodhi. Why? Affliction is born of ignorance and karmic consciousness, bodhi grows from purity and compassion; yet consciousness and wisdom are neither one nor two. Why is this? Consciousness is false, wisdom is true; apart from the true there is no false, apart from the false there is no true. Living beings are deluded about the true and chase the false, and so affliction arises; the deeper the affliction, the farther from the true. But if the aspiration is genuine and the grinding deep, then suddenly one recognizes that consciousness and the false are illusion; advancing, one does not separate from the illusion but takes the illusion as true; advancing further, one does not cling to the true, and at once is cool — consciousness becomes wisdom. For the suffering and joy of the world have originally no self-nature; what is called suffering and what is called joy are both imposed by the karmic consciousness and deluded mind in its own discrimination. Take it as suffering and it is suffering; take it as joy and it is joy. Thus in the arena of fame and profit, where men rush and serve, the ardent take it as joy while the lofty-minded take it as suffering. In the halls of song and dance, with lanterns red and wine green, the self-restrained take it as suffering while the dissolute take it as joy. So Hanshan wandered at ease among the rocky crags and found the swill sweet as fine fare; Shide worked in the kitchen and turned laughter and talk into joy; Huisi of Nanyue, through illness, recognized the illusion and at once turned to lightness and ease; and even Yanzi with his basket and gourd in a mean alley — others could not bear his sorrow, yet Yanzi did not change his joy. From this one may know that affliction and bodhi are both one mind and have originally no self-nature, and that to be able to turn affliction into bodhi is the meaning of turning consciousness into wisdom.

Now that you understand the meaning of affliction-bodhi, you should not fear suffering or hardship, but seek joy within suffering and hardship — only that is true joy. The reason people of the world shrink from hardship and seek ease, fear suffering and run after joy, is that consciousness obstructs wisdom. If one can know that all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, one will not of oneself take suffering as suffering and cling to it, or take joy as joy and cling to it. Yet even so, if one does not grind through suffering and hardship one item at a time, then when suffering comes one still clings to suffering, and when joy comes one still clings to joy, and the karmic consciousness is still hard to break through — how then can one turn consciousness into wisdom? And without turning consciousness into wisdom, how can a lotus be born in fire? From this one may know that the two meanings, a lotus born in fire and turning consciousness into wisdom, are mutually functioning — only this is the true meaning of affliction-bodhi. The student of the Buddha Dharma should take these two meanings as a motto at his side and constantly use them to encourage himself.

Fellow students, now that you understand this meaning, do not lightly take the phrase affliction-bodhi to mean that affliction is bodhi. To take it so at once is to mislead oneself. Why? Affliction is suffering, bodhi is joy, and suffering is not joy. Affliction is dark, bodhi is bright, and dark is not bright. Affliction is karmic deluded consciousness, bodhi is the pure true mind, and the false is not the true. Those of the ordinary mouth-Chan mostly borrow the phrase “affliction is bodhi” to think that one awakening finishes everything, and become arrogant and self-conceited, disdaining practice in actual fact. They little realize that until one has reached the great, thorough awakening, how can one lightly speak of the false as the true, or equate affliction with bodhi? Therefore the beginner in the Buddha Dharma must on no account say that affliction is bodhi; he may only say that without affliction there is no bodhi.

Why? Bodhi is the awakened mind, and affliction is the good teacher that rouses the awakened mind. For human life is like a dream, like dwelling in a dark room. Only because one is in the dark does the wish to seek light arise. Only because of affliction does the mind that loathes and leaves affliction arise. On that day Śākyamuni Buddha, because he saw the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death, made the vow not to return to the royal palace until the eight sufferings were ended and not to attain right awakening until he had — and even went through five more years of seeking the Way and six years in the Snow Mountains with the suffering of one sesame seed and one grain of wheat a day, before he perfected bodhi. Yet living beings day after day are in the bitter sea of birth, death, and affliction, clinging to delusion and not awakening; not only can they not recognize affliction as a good teacher, but within affliction they create more affliction. And those who have a little awakening, not knowing the wonderful meaning of a lotus born in fire and turning consciousness into wisdom, plant only causes with outflows and greedily seek blessings in a future life. They little realize that blessings are enough to obstruct bodhi. Why? Great blessing means great karma too, and great karma means deep obstruction; with great karma and deep obstruction, one is farther still from the road of bodhi. Therefore it is not called blessing-bodhi but affliction-bodhi. The Sixth Patriarch said: “The deluded cultivate blessings but not the Way, saying only that cultivating blessings is the Way; they think to cultivate blessings to wipe out their offenses, but when a later life wins blessings, the offense is still there.” This is the meaning of blessings obstructing bodhi.

A student of the Buddha Dharma does not wholly cast away blessings, but he should know that such blessings are the result of good causes with outflows from former lives, and when the reward is exhausted he falls again. Therefore having blessings, he does not think of them as blessings. Not thinking of them as blessings means not thinking of enjoying them himself, but turning them to the spreading of the Dharma and the benefit of living beings, to the completing of people and things. In this way the greater his blessings, the greater his merit. If he seeks only his own enjoyment, then once the good reward is exhausted the evil reward comes, and regret will be too late. Rather than enjoy a limited blessing and suffer boundless evil reward, why not base oneself on the practice of benefiting others without self and quickly ascend the shore of awakening?

The student of the Buddha Dharma should have far sight and a great measure of mind; he should not crave small gains nor rest content with the old ways. You should know that without great giving there is no great gain; without great suffering there is no great joy. The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One came by it through great giving and great suffering. Hence Mencius said: “When Heaven is about to lay a great task on a man, it must first bitter his heart and mind, toil his sinews and bones, starve his body and skin, and empty his person, and thwart and confound whatever he does.” From this one sees that not only is it so in studying the Buddha Dharma; even in worldly dharmas, one who would bear a great task must pass through just such affliction. Nor is it only those who bear great tasks: something as small as making a name for oneself, or mastering a single skill, and even all the inventions of science, none can succeed without long grinding, deep study, and bitter thought. As the saying goes: “A troubled state brings forth loyal ministers; a poor household brings forth filial children; a strict teacher brings forth high disciples; a thatched hut brings forth dukes and ministers.” All of these are the principle of gaining joy through suffering; hence affliction-bodhi. I hope you will see this point clearly: to accept adversity with compliance, and to be non-dual in adversity and compliance — that is utmost sincerity. As it is said, “Only the utmost sincerity under heaven can transform” — not only transforming affliction into bodhi, but transforming and saving all.

blocks.text: Tenth Sitting: The Causality of the Three Times

inline.s: Fellow students, there is nothing else in studying the Buddha Dharma: at root one must understand causality. The way of cause and effect is not off by a hair; not only can good and evil retribution not escape the law of causality, but all the myriad appearances of the universe are no exception. The immeasurable Dharma gates the Buddha taught are the explanation of the principle of causality. All the rise and fall, survival and ruin in the world are the proof of the fact of causality. The deluded do not understand this principle, and as soon as they hear the word causality they either despise it as superstitious nonsense or take it as a divine mystery beyond knowing. And so those who despise it deny causality altogether, and those who take it as unknowable go against causality. For this reason the Buddha Dharma has not flourished, and the world's ways and people's minds grow more shallow by the day — truly a matter for sighing.

The principle of the two words cause and effect is quite evident. Take the seasons: sunrise and sunset are the cause, day and night the effect; cold is the cause, frost and snow the effect. Take human affairs: internal injury and external attack are the cause, illness the effect; study is the cause, knowledge the effect; diligence and thrift are the cause, wealth the effect; extravagance and laziness are the cause, poverty the effect. Take science: in physics, heat and cold are the cause, contraction and expansion the effect; in chemistry, one part oxygen and two parts hydrogen are the cause, the forming of water the effect; in mathematics, multiplication and division are the cause, product and quotient the effect. And even he who loves others is constantly loved, and he who kills others is constantly killed — there is not one thing that is not a phenomenon of cause and effect. How can it be called superstition, and how is it obscure and hard to know? In truth there is no moment when we do not live within the law of causality; it is we ourselves who are dreaming. Yet the principle of causality, though evident, is subtle, and though simple, is complex. Why? Considered in one matter or one thing, causality is simple and evident, as in the examples from seasons, human affairs, and science given above. But considered in terms of human good and evil, causes and conditions arise mutually, subtle and complex, cycling without end, and unless one understands the causality of past, present, and future — the three times — one cannot know its reasons deeply.

Let me use the melon as a figure. The melon seed is a figure for the cause, the melon for the effect. The melon of the present is born of the seed of the past, and the seed of the present gives birth to the melon of the future. This figures how the effect of the present is born of the cause of the past, and the cause of the present gives birth to the effect of the future; the causality of human life is just the same. Yet the same melon seed, sown in different places, gives melons that differ in quality, in earliness or lateness, in size, in sweetness — this is because outside the cause there are conditions: conditions help the cause to arise, and the cause depends on conditions to appear; when causes and conditions differ, the effects differ. Thus a single kind of seed already contains latent causes of better and worse: the better cause yields a better fruit, the worse cause a worse fruit — this is simple causality. At sowing time, if the seed is good and the fertilizer plentiful, the good cause meets a good condition, and so a good fruit is formed; if the seed is good but the fertilizer scanty, then the cause is good but meets a poor condition, and the fruit differs. If the seed is poor and the fertilizer plentiful, then the poor cause meets a good condition and the fruit too is rather good. Conversely, poor cause and poor condition give an even worse fruit. As for differences of weather, of hoeing and weeding, and of diligence or slackness in irrigation, each and every one affects the changes of cause and effect. In sum, from cause to effect one must wait upon conditions, and the differences among conditions are very great. Therefore the matter of causality is evident yet subtle, simple yet complex, and not at all easy to know.

Even in the small matter of melons and fruits, cause and effect are not easy to know; how much less the causality of human life, subtle and manifold — how could the fleshly eye of an ordinary being peer into its beginnings? The deluded do not examine this, but measure causality solely by success and failure, gain and loss in the present life: as if the good got evil reward and the evil got good reward, the strong always strong and the weak always weak. And in recent years, in floods, droughts, and other calamities, the poor and honest folk in the countryside have suffered most, while the rich and idle in the cities have suffered least — and so they suspect that causality has no basis. Is this not a great confusion? You should know that causality runs through the three times: the good person's good reward and the evil person's evil reward are simple causality; the good person's evil reward and the evil person's good reward are complex causality. As for the good person who gets an evil reward: the evil cause from a former life ripens first in this life; though he is good in this life, he has no supremely great merit, and the evil cause of the former life cannot be avoided, and so he receives an evil reward — but his good cause in this life will still form a good fruit in a future life. As for the evil person who gets a good reward: the good cause from a former life ripens first in this life; though he is evil in this life, he is not heinously wicked, and the good cause of the former life cannot be wiped out, and so he receives a good reward — but his evil cause in this life will still form an evil fruit in a future life. There are also those whose good and evil rewards differ within a single life, and this too is because of the differing causes and conditions of good and evil in past lives and this life, and so the rewards differ. The same holds for the strong and the weak. Those who suffer in the countryside: by an evil cause from a former life they are born in the countryside in this life, enduring poverty and hardship, or suffering further calamity; but those who have the habit of honesty and diligence are planting good causes for a future life. Those who live at ease in the cities: by a good cause from a former life they are born in the cities in this life, enjoying better things, or escaping calamity; but those who have the evil habits of arrogance, luxury, and license are planting further evil causes for a future life. As it is said, doing good brings down auspiciousness and doing evil brings down calamity; the household that accumulates goodness must have abundant blessings, and the household that accumulates evil must have abundant misfortune. These matters of causal cycling are no different from the causality and conditions of planting a melon and getting a melon, better and worse, fat and lean.

As the histories record: Bai Qi buried alive the soldiers of Zhao, and after long sinking into the hells to suffer, was reborn as a daughter of the Chen family in Jiangnan (see the Yijian Zhi), and afterward fell into the body of a centipede (see the Quntan Caiyu). Empress Lü poisoned Liu Ruyi, Prince of Zhao, and Ruyi's ghost injured her armpit so that she died (see the Records of the Grand Historian

The Basic Annals of Empress Dowager Lü). Cao Cao himself carried out usurpation and betrayed people all his life, and for many lives was reborn as a pig (see the notebooks of earlier writers). An Lushan usurped the Tang and killed its sons and grandsons, and went blind and diseased with sores, and was in turn usurped by Shi Siming (see the New Book of Tang

Biographies of Treacherous Ministers). Yuan Ang slandered and killed Chao Cuo; for ten lives Ang was an eminent monk, and when he was reborn as National Master Wuda, Chao Cuo became a human-faced sore to haunt him (see the Biographies of Eminent Monks). Lü Mengzheng silently prayed for descendants who would protect the Buddha Dharma; for three generations afterward they were ministers and devout believers in the Buddha Dharma (see the Jintang Pian). Lady Xi, through hatred and jealousy, fell into the body of a python (see the Biographies of Eminent Monks). Wang Hua, father of Master Yangming, refused beautiful women and took first place in the empire (see the Yuanjian Leihan). Yang Hu's former body was a son of the Li family (see the Book of Jin

The Biography of Yang Hu). Shi Kefa was the rebirth of Wen Tianxiang (see the Biography of Shi Kefa). Records such as these are too many to relate. And in recent years the matters of karmic retribution have been even more evident. The causality of the three times is clear and well attested — how can it be denied!

You should know that in the relation of cause and effect, not only are the facts that are plainly recorded never off by a hair, but within a single thought cause and effect are already present. The ancient worthies said: Think of the Buddha and you are Buddha; think of Mara and you are Mara. They also said: one thought makes you a Buddha. Conversely, one thought makes you a Mara. From of old there is no telling how many practitioners have fallen through a single thought. And in worldly dharmas, no one can tell how many have damaged their blessings through a single thought, or turned danger into safety through a single thought. Take our own practice: one whose practice is deep, if he stirs a thought for a moment and that thought is impure, or if he feels a little weariness, receives retribution at once — lightly, strange pain on the seat; more heavily, illness or some other complication. If he repents with utmost sincerity, he immediately returns to calm. Why? When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease — as it is said, when the cause arises the effect arises, and when the cause ceases the effect ceases. For those whose practice is deep have purer mind-thoughts than beginners; if once they are impure, that single thought is at once cause and effect — like a radio broadcast filling the void; in the field of the eighth consciousness cause and effect are established at once, and so the response is so swift.

Since we know that causality is never destroyed, then in the stirring of the mind and the arising of thoughts, and in meeting matters and handling things, we should work on the cause at every point: not giving rise to evil thoughts, not doing crooked deeds. As it is said, do no evil and practice all good — only thus does one count as a person who truly understands causality. If the mouth is good while the mind is evil, if words do not match deeds and deeds do not match words, then not only is it hard to deceive the gods, but how can one escape the causality of one's own mind? By a single evil thought the evil cause is already planted and the evil fruit already set; one creates the cause oneself and receives the retribution oneself — what need is there for the gods to reward and punish? Yet people of the world dream on, full of greed, hatred, doubt, and delusion, seeking only a moment's pleasure, deceiving their hearts and blinding themselves, heedless of what comes after. And when the evil fruit ripens, they blame heaven and resent others, and their confusion grows worse, planting new evil causes upon the evil fruit, with retribution without end — truly a matter for sorrowful sighs. Therefore it is said: “The bodhisattva fears the cause, living beings fear the effect.” The bodhisattva fears the cause because, such being the cause, such will be the effect. Living beings fear the effect because they do not understand that such an effect is born of such a cause. Therefore cause is effect and effect is cause.

Fellow students, the student of the Buddha Dharma must not only understand causality but must turn causality around. What is turning? Turning from the cause. If the cause can be turned, the effect turns with the cause — as it is said, the fifth, eighth, sixth, and seventh consciousnesses turn in respect of effect and cause. To turn affliction into bodhi, to turn the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms, one must begin from the cause. The sixth consciousness creates karma; when the sixth consciousness is turned, then thought after thought is self-aware, and not only does one create no evil cause, but one repents with utmost sincerity the offenses of past and present. The seventh consciousness grasps a self; when the seventh consciousness is turned, then not only is there no self, but one bases oneself on the great vow and great practice to benefit others. In this way karmic obstructions dissolve day by day and merit advances day by day, and all afflictions and evil causes are turned into bodhi's good fruit. At the same time, one should arouse the aspiration to turn the causality of shared karma as well. For instance, the natural and man-made calamities of successive years are created by the shared karma of living beings; one should set an example by one's own ceasing of evil and doing of good, and urge people everywhere to cease from evil and do good, and together turn evil causes into good causes and evil fruit into good fruit. Only with such a mind does one count as a disciple of the Tathāgata.

You should know that the source of all causality of good and evil arises in the mind-thoughts. Therefore think of the ordinary and you are ordinary; think of the sage and you are a sage. As it is said: in spring you sow a single grain of millet, in autumn you reap ten thousand seeds; the good and evil a person does return in retribution just so. How great, then, is the causality of mind-thoughts! In practicing this mind-ground Dharma, you must not only understand the harm and benefit of causality, but should thoroughly turn around the causality of your own mind; only then can you escape birth and death. Therefore in my recorded sayings it is said: the Buddha Dharma is a record of cause and effect, a Dharma gate for escaping birth and death.

blocks.text: Eleventh Sitting: The Perfect Harmony of Principle and Practice

inline.s: Fellow students, in the Buddha Dharma there is a distinction between practice and principle. Studying and expounding the scriptures and treatises is called principle; practicing according to the Dharma is called practice. The phrase “mind itself is Buddha” also has a distinction of practice and principle, and the student must understand it clearly. Yet practice and principle are fundamentally not two: one must penetrate practice by principle and reveal principle through practice. When practice and principle are one suchness, then practice is principle and principle is practice, and only then can one say that mind itself is Buddha. If one suddenly says, “mind itself is Buddha,” does one mean the Buddha in practice or the Buddha in principle? If it is the Buddha in practice, then one should actually walk the Buddha Way and prove it in practice; if it is not proved in practice, then it is still the Buddha in principle — no more than an empty, hollow ideal.

The ancient worthies of the Chan school, in their great compassion, feared that students would go wrong in searching after principle and only increase their views; and so, cutting through nails and slicing through iron, they smashed all theories, forbade reading the sutras and forbade lecturing on the teachings — all to teach people to penetrate solely through practice. Only when practice is penetrated can the mind be understood. At the Avataṃsaka assembly Śākyamuni Buddha taught the one true Dharma realm, the principle of inexhaustible dependent origination, concealing within it the meaning that mind itself is Buddha. But those of small capacity saw as if they had not seen and heard as if they had not heard, and so in skillful means he turned to teach the Small Vehicle. Then from the Small Vehicle he led them toward the Great Vehicle, slowly leading them up to the mind. Then he taught prajñā, breaking all obstructions of principle and of practice. Finally, at the Lotus assembly, he gathered the three into one, and with the non-dual way of the One Vehicle made clear the principle that mind itself is Buddha. All his provisional and skillful means were no more than to make people understand that mind itself is Buddha and to teach them to break all clinging. You should know that the three baskets and twelve divisions of sutras and treatises, and the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, are all principle. Therefore all scriptures and teachings are called the principle of the teaching. If one does not accomplish practice according to principle, what value are these scriptures? And if one can reveal principle through practice, why cling to these scriptures? This is the reason the ancient worthies of the Chan school forbade reading the sutras and even reviled the Buddha and cursed the patriarchs. Otherwise, not to lecture on the scriptures and even to revile them — would that not be slandering the Buddha and destroying the Dharma? Could that still be the Buddha Dharma? Only because ordinary beings love to cling: once they cling to the scriptures, all kinds of obstructions of principle arise, and the deeper they cling to principle, the farther they are from practice. Therefore the worthies cut off views and opinions and worked solely on practice; when practice is penetrated, principle is complete of itself, and one can naturally awaken to the Buddha of one's own mind.

The eight words of the Chan school, “the path of speech is cut off, the place of mental activity is extinguished,” are of the greatest importance. Think: when the path is cut off and the mind extinguished, what realm is that? Is there still any principle to speak of? The ancients were loyal and sincere and had true faith in their teachers; they simply acted according to their teachers' words without exhausting the principle, and so they saw the nature very quickly. Later people's doubt and delusion are too heavy, and they love to discuss principle; the more principle, the more obstruction, and wishing to seek liberation they only add obstruction to obstruction and bond to bond — is this not greatly to be lamented?

Fellow students, one who studies the Buddha Dharma must possess great wisdom. One of great wisdom knows that the Chan school is thoroughgoing and strikes blood at a single prick. One of small wisdom, not understanding the principle of the provisional and the real, clings to the vow “the Dharma gates are immeasurable, I vow to learn them all,” and so gropes east and gropes west, never working on his own mind. He little realizes that the Dharma gates of his own mind are originally immeasurable, and that all Dharma gates do not go outside his own mind. Since all dharmas do not go outside one's own mind, why did our Buddha trouble to teach all the scriptures so broadly? Only because living beings abandon the root and chase the branches, turn their backs on awakening and join with dust, and so live and die in vain, beguiled of their original mind. Therefore the Buddha taught all kinds of dharmas to cure the many kinds of deluded mind of living beings, all to lead them back from the false to the true and to see the Buddha of their own mind. If a person of great capacity and great wisdom hears once and understands a thousand things, at once stills the mad mind, and as soon as he arouses bodhi becomes a right-awakened one, breathing through the same nostril as the buddhas of the three times — then all scriptures and teachings are wholly in this mind, inexhaustible and unfailing, and why should he seek outwardly? The ancient worthy said: “The Buddha taught all dharmas to cure all minds. I have no such minds; what use have I for all dharmas?” From this one sees that all dharmas are the Buddha's words of skillful means. The Diamond Sutra says: “If anyone says the Tathāgata has a Dharma to teach, he slanders the Buddha.” It also says: “The teacher of the Dharma has no Dharma to teach; that is called teaching the Dharma.” If the student of the Buddha Dharma understands this meaning, he will naturally not seek the Dharma outside the mind and add further obstruction of principle.

Someone may say: “The sutras were spoken by the Buddha; if a practitioner leaves the scriptures behind, what is the Buddha Dharma?” You little realize that the Buddha's principle is deep and hard to understand, and that to interpret the meaning merely by the text is to mistake the finger for the moon. Even if one can grasp the meaning apart from the text, it is still an empty principle, like a hungry man talking about food, which does not fill him. Therefore in the Śūraṅgama Sutra the Buddha told Ānanda: “Though for kalpas you remember and hold the Tathāgata's secret, wonderful adornment, it is not equal to one day's cultivation of the outflow-free work.” The words of the Chan school strike blood at a single prick, with no room for detour or wavering. Many of the ancient worthies awakened through a single word from their teacher. The teacher said the mind is Buddha, and they believed the mind is Buddha. The teacher said the mind cannot be grasped, and they believed the mind cannot be grasped. Their faith in the teacher was genuine and their doubt and delusion dissolved, and so they awakened at the word. This is the actual benefit of transmitting mind by mind. Later people's minds gradually departed from simplicity, and so the practice was changed to investigating a huatou. The student, following only the one phrase his teacher gave him, a phrase about which nothing can be reasoned, goes on reciting and investigating it whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; not only does he get a beating with the incense board for reading the sutras, but he also gets one for departing from the root huatou his teacher gave him. When he has investigated to the point where the mountains end and the rivers run out, and suddenly it opens through, he awakens to the truth that his own mind is Buddha, and all matters of practice and principle become thoroughly clear. At that point, what scripture is there that he may not read, and what obstruction of principle can arise?

Fellow students, the buddhas of the three times all attained accomplishment through holding the Esoteric. But the Esoteric Dharma gives even more weight to practice in actual fact and not to theory. For example, the Mahāvairocana Sutra and the Vajraśekhara Sutra both give weight to practice in actual fact, and other esoteric sutras likewise; and they have all kinds of rituals and adorned sanctuaries, the purpose being to make the student arouse reverence and faith, and to gather in the mind through practice until it returns to one. The Esoteric Dharma gives the greatest weight to the vajra guru: one relies only on the guru's oral transmission, with no meaning to reason about. Moreover, for the same esoteric mantra, the sound transmitted by different gurus often differs, and the student should follow the sound transmitted by his own teacher; only then is there response. Though the sounds differ, the response is one — is there still any principle to discuss?

From what has been said above, one can see that both the Chan and Esoteric schools give weight to practice and do not cling to principle; they rely only on the person and not on the Dharma. What I, Huiming, said earlier about relying on the Dharma and not on the person was because I was ashamed that my own merit was insufficient and feared increasing my arrogance. In truth, in studying Chan and Esoteric one gives weight only to the teacher's transmission and doubts nothing at all; only then is there benefit.

As the saying goes: “The obstruction of practice obstructs ordinary beings; the obstruction of principle obstructs bodhisattvas.” You should know that the obstruction of principle obstructs bodhisattvas at the causal stage; a bodhisattva at the fruition stage is certainly not obstructed by principle. When the Sixth Patriarch heard the Fifth Patriarch transmit the sutra, he awakened at once — where was there any obstruction of principle? All the ancient worthies who awakened to the Way were not obstructed by principle. For one penetrates the obstruction of practice by principle, and the obstruction of principle by practice; if one cannot make practice and principle one suchness, how can one be called a bodhisattva? In studying the Buddha Dharma, one should first study and weigh carefully every Dharma gate and see whether its road is right or not, and must not follow blindly — this is the key. If the road is right, then one should penetrate deeply through one gate and practice according to the Dharma, and no longer cling to principle.

Fellow students, the Buddha Dharma and worldly dharmas are both different and not different. How are they different? There is the difference of giving weight to views and not giving weight to views. Worldly dharmas give weight to views: the more one sees and hears, the more one studies and investigates, the more one is called profound and learned. But with many views, the mind of discrimination is heavy and the view of self and other deep, and conflicts grow worse still. The strife of theories and the strife for fame and profit — from what do they arise if not this? The Buddha Dharma puts first the breaking of views, for worldly wisdom and clever argument is one of the eight difficulties: it is the hardest to enter the Way with it and it obstructs the Way most severely. Therefore one must forget the mechanism and rest the views. When the mechanism is forgotten and the views are rested, then the obstructions of principle and of practice are broken together, and one is without hindrance and at ease — hence they are said to be different.

How are they not different? In giving weight to practice and to action they are not different. In worldly dharmas, reading books and lecturing on learning are valued for practical use. If one hugs a dead book and can only sit and talk but not rise and act, then though one be versed in antiquity and modern times, it has nothing to do with reality. Hence the Confucians say: “If a man honors the worthy and sets aside beauty, serves his parents with all his strength, serves his lord with his life, and in dealings with friends is true to his word — though men say he has not learned, I must call him learned.” From of old, loyal ministers and filial sons, worthy mothers and chaste wives, all came by it through earnest personal practice — how could mere talk and theory produce them? In the Buddha Dharma, faith, vow, and practice, the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, must likewise be practiced in actual fact to be of benefit. And as for being at ease in adversity and prosperity and giving rise to no affliction, that can be shown in no other way than through practice — hence they are said not to be different.

In the true principle of the Buddha Dharma, even the mind cannot be found — how could worldly knowledge and worldly views understand it? If another strikes me or scolds me, the ordinary being takes him as an enemy, while the student of the Buddha Dharma takes him as a good teacher. Poverty, hardship, sickness, and adversity the ordinary being counts as bad, while the student of the Buddha Dharma counts as good. Fame, profit, and respect the ordinary being counts as good, while the student of the Buddha Dharma counts as bad. For the ordinary being does not understand the relation of cause and effect, and measures enmity and kindness, good and bad, only by what is before his eyes. The Buddha Dharma, basing itself on the principle of causal cycling, regards all as equal. Thus to be struck and scolded can dissolve past karma; poverty, hardship, sickness, and adversity can give rise to bodhi; fame, profit, and respect can obstruct bodhi. Therefore it is said that good is bad and bad is good. In such matters the views of the Buddha Dharma and of worldly dharmas are thus opposed — can one still cling and reason? If one would reason, one must reason according to the Buddha's principle; only that is true principle.

In the dual practice of Chan and Esoteric, one does not cling to principle but gives sole weight to practice, penetrating principle through practice, and principle is then complete. If one can practice according to the Dharma, being compassionate in every matter and pure in every thought, what principle is not present? If one clings to principle and abandons practice, principle becomes a painted cake; though one be widely versed in the teachings and eloquent as a rushing stream, if one's action contradicts one's words and self-clinging and affliction increase rather than decrease, where is the principle then? Therefore practice and principle are not two: it is by practice that one penetrates principle, not by principle that one encompasses practice. I hope you will take note.

blocks.text: Twelfth Sitting: No Vehicle, Pure Land

inline.s: Fellow students, in the Buddha Dharma every dharma is equal and all have merit; there is fundamentally no division of Great Vehicle and Small Vehicle. The Tathāgata set up teachings as remedies to fit the disease: because living beings' karmic consciousness differs, their measure of mind is great or small, and so in skillful means he guided them, teaching the small and the great. In truth, returning to the source is not two; only the Pure Land Dharma gate covers all three capacities and gathers in both the sharp and the dull, so that sages above and ordinary beings below alike ascend the shore of awakening. For the Pure Land takes the four characters Amitābha Buddha as its true sutra — as it is said, “One phrase of Amitābha is the king of dharmas.” Since the Pure Land Dharma gate is so excellent, why did the Tathāgata establish the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates besides? You should know that living beings' capacities differ and their conditions are various; without many gates of skillful means, how could all be gathered in? But all dharmas flow out from the Pure Land Dharma realm and return again to the Pure Land Dharma ocean, and when one returns to the source, not one dharma can be found. As for the Buddha's speaking of the West, this is the meaning of using the sun as a figure. Why? The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is a figure for the place where human life returns. Therefore when a practitioner passes away it is called returning west. In truth the Pure Land pervades the Dharma realm, boundless and without limit — how could there be east and west, directions and positions? It is only that living beings' faculties are sharp or dull: to those of sharp faculties and great measure of mind the Buddha taught the Great Vehicle; to those of dull faculties and small measure of mind he taught the Small Vehicle; and to those who do not understand their own mind but greedily seek a Buddha outside, he taught, as a remedy to fit the disease, the Western Pure Land, using delusion to dispel delusion. In truth all Dharma gates are not apart from one's own mind, and so the ultimate Pure Land is precisely in one's own mind. When the mind is pure the land is pure; when the mind is defiled the land is defiled. The cultivation of any Dharma gate can purify the mind; one need not practice only the Pure Land Dharma gate to return to the Pure Land — as it is said, all is one.

Fellow students, apart from the Pure Land of one's own mind, is there after all a Western Pure Land? You should know that there certainly is. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sutra — all three sutras tell of the adorned and majestic matters of the Western Pure Land, direct and dependent, vivid as a painting; and the great-vehicle sutras and treatises all likewise praise the Pure Land. The buddhas and bodhisattvas certainly do not speak falsely, and we may deeply believe without doubt. But the Western Pure Land is manifested by mind only: if one's own mind is not pure, the Western Pure Land is separated by a hundred thousand million buddha-lands — how could one reach it? If one's own mind can be pure, then the Western Pure Land is not separated by so much as a hair's tip, and one arrives as soon as the thought is made. Therefore when one's own mind is pure, the Pure Land of one's own mind is the Western Buddha-land. Hence the ancient worthy said: “Recite the Buddha, recite the mind, the mind recites the Buddha.” From this one sees that Buddha is mind and mind is Buddha; reciting the Buddha is reciting the mind, and reciting the mind is reciting the Buddha. If one clings to being born in the West, one is one-sidedly attached to direction and position and loses the original mind. That being so, is there still the matter of being born in the West? You should know that as to birth, one is certainly born; as to going, one in truth does not go. Therefore the ancient worthies, at the point of death, mostly recited the Buddha's name — not out of clinging and seeking to be born in the West, but because reciting the Buddha is being Buddha.

The Pure Land Dharma gate has four kinds of practice: first, recitation of the name; second, contemplation of the image; third, contemplation of the thought; fourth, recitation of the mark of reality. Most who practice the Pure Land Dharma gate cultivate only the recitation of the name. If one can recite the name to the point of single-mindedness unconfused, then a thousand practitioners and a thousand go, and there truly is a West to be born in. Therefore one who recites the name should have true faith and earnest vow, and recite until the moment of death, when he cannot manage any other thought and only this one thought of the Buddha remains; then he moves Amitābha Buddha to come and receive and guide him, and he is certainly born in the West. Also, one who did not know to recite the Buddha in ordinary life, if at the point of death the good roots of past kalpas suddenly burst forth and he can suddenly recite, can also be born in the West. But ordinarily those born in the West are said to be born there carrying their karma. What is carrying karma? Not only the unfinished karma of past kalpas and this life, but even this single thought of reciting the Buddha, if not yet purified, is also called karma. Why is reciting the Buddha also karma? Because every thought is delusion, and every thought is impure. Therefore one who cultivates the Pure Land is said to cultivate pure karma. Whoever is born in the West carrying karma must, after birth there, practice still further. As for one whose mouth recites while the mind goes against it, he only plants good roots and cannot yet be born in the West. Why? Because in ordinary days he did not recite with a true mind, and at the point of death, when a hundred feelings crowd together, no thought of the Buddha arises in his mind, and he cannot recite. That so many people in the world recite the Buddha while so few are born in the West is for this very reason. As for contemplation of the image and contemplation of the thought, these are still skillful means of gathering the mind by objects, and are still not ultimate. Why? The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is delusion.” If one awakens to non-arising, one realizes the mark of reality. Only when the mark of reality is realized is it ultimate. The mark of reality is markless — what is there to contemplate or think? Only the recitation of the mark of reality does not cling to the mark of the land, does not cling to the mark of the Buddha, does not cling to the mark of reciting. Reciting the Buddha is being Buddha — that is recitation of the mark of reality. When it reaches the point of reciting without reciting and not reciting while reciting, that is the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. When one recites to the point where the “I” that recites and the “he” that is recited are both nothing whatsoever, then reciter and recited are both forgotten, the mark of reality appears before one, and without waiting for Amitābha to receive and guide one, one realizes markless bodhi.

According to what has been said above, why should the student of the Buddha Dharma not abandon the small and turn to the great? What is small and great? Reciting the Buddha merely to seek birth in the West is small; reciting the Buddha of the mark of reality is great. For reciting the Buddha is good in itself, but as soon as one seeks birth in the West, it belongs to marks. With marks there is abiding, and with abiding there is measure. Having measure, it is called small. In reciting the Buddha of the mark of reality, one recites until the true mind beyond thought is wholly revealed, and one realizes the mark of reality. The mark of reality is markless, immeasurable, and boundless, and so it is called great. Moreover, one who is born in the West carrying karma must still return to the Sahā world to walk the bodhisattva path. But one who recites the Buddha of the mark of reality — reciting the Buddha is being Buddha, this body is Buddha, and one walks the Buddha Way — is that not more excellent? Even so, the realm of reciting the Buddha of the mark of reality is too high; one whose capacity does not correspond may recite the Diamond Sutra more often, and will then be able to awaken to reciting the Buddha of the mark of reality. Why? This sutra is the prajñā of the mark of reality, sufficient to perfume and bring forth one's prajñā seeds, and so one can break marks and see the nature. Otherwise one may choose one of the three methods — recitation of the name, contemplation of the image, contemplation of the thought — and practice it with single-mindedness, and one should be able to be born in the West. In this age of the Dharma's ending, whoever one may be, if one can recite a single phrase of the holy name “Namo Amitābha Buddha,” one plants good roots and gains immeasurable merit.

Fellow students, the ultimate aim in studying the Buddha Dharma is only to seek a pure mind. Every Dharma gate can purify the mind. Every Dharma gate is a Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation. Why? Because every Dharma gate accomplishes the Buddha Way. And every Dharma gate is Chan. Why? Because Chan gives weight to one's own mind. If in any Dharma gate one does not understand one's own mind, one will in the end not accomplish it, for outside the mind there is no dharma. Take the Pure Land Dharma gate: when one recites the name to the point of single-mindedness unconfused, is that state not Chan? The Contemplation Sutra says: “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.” If that is not Chan, what is? In reciting the Buddha of the mark of reality, when samādhi appears before one, one enters right concentration — is that not Chan too? Therefore the verse in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sutra says: “If a person simply recites Amitābha Buddha, this is called the supreme, profound, wonderful Chan.” Since it is called reciting the Buddha, why is it also called profound and wonderful Chan? From this one sees that reciting the Buddha is Chan. Furthermore, the Pure Land and the Esoteric Dharma are also equal without difference. Why? The four characters Amitābha Buddha are the total retention of all sutras; total retention is the meaning of esoteric mantra. To recite Amitābha Buddha, if one does not think of the land and does not think of the Buddha, is equal to holding an esoteric mantra. Again, the recitation of the name, contemplation of the image, and contemplation of the thought in the Pure Land Dharma gate are no different from the holding of mantras and visualization at the beginning stage of the Esoteric Dharma; and the recitation of the mark of reality in the Pure Land Dharma gate, in which reciter and recited are both forgotten, is no different from the prajñā of the Esoteric Dharma. Only, the esoteric practitioner enters gradually in order, while the Pure Land practitioner chooses one of the four kinds of Buddha-recitation and cultivates it exclusively. From this one can see that Chan is Pure Land and Pure Land is Esoteric — as it is said, three yet one, one yet three, one is all, all is one; what distinction is there? Later people, not understanding these principles, insist on dividing the schools by mere names and contend with one another over great and small — all of it is clinging to marks and binding oneself. In truth the ultimate of the Buddha Dharma has no great or small, and nothing can be spoken of; all that is spoken returns to the One Vehicle. For when Buddha-recitation reaches the point where samādhi appears, when Chan investigation reaches the end of the huatou, when esoteric practice reaches the one suchness of the three mysteries, the return to the source is not two — all is but the purifying of the mind.

The Buddha Dharma has many gates, yet all alike give weight to keeping the precepts. Though the categories of precepts are many, they come down to two: bodily precepts and mind precepts — that is, the precept against reckless bodily action and the precept against deluded thought. Whether Great Vehicle or Small Vehicle, whoever can keep the precepts is of the Buddha Dharma; whoever cannot keep the precepts is not of the Buddha Dharma. Only, the Great and Small Vehicles have very many categories of precepts, each with its own emphasis. One who practices the Great Vehicle, because he complies with all and benefits others according to conditions, gives weight to the mind precepts. One who practices the Small Vehicle, because he guards the Tathāgata's family estate and must be pure and adorned in the four dignified deportments so that people of the world respect the Buddha Dharma, gives weight to the bodily precepts. As for the fundamental five precepts — against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants — laypeople mostly undertake them. But whether Great Vehicle precepts, Small Vehicle precepts, or lay precepts, whoever can truly undertake and keep them not only has great merit but can move others to believe in the Buddha Dharma. If one undertakes but does not keep them, one not only invites the offense of breaking the precepts, but moves people of the world to doubt and slander the Buddha Dharma, and even affects the faith of ordinary students of the Buddha Dharma. If you understand this principle, you will see that one who can keep the precepts does well to study the Great Vehicle and does well to study the Small Vehicle; while one who cannot keep the precepts, whether he studies the great or the small, is not only wrong in every way but must surely fall. The mind-ground Dharma we study is the markless Dharma gate of the Great Vehicle, and one must keep the precept of a mind-ground without wrong; otherwise one will not only fall but will be seized by Mara in this very body.

Next, the Small Vehicle's bodily precepts lean toward marks, while the Great Vehicle's mind precepts do not abide in marks. What leans toward marks is easy to see; what does not abide in marks is hard to know. Just because it is hard to know, one should be all the more guarded and careful about what one does not see, and fearful about what one does not hear — compared with what leans toward marks, the difference in difficulty cannot be measured in miles. The bodily and mental categories of precepts described above differ in difficulty, but the merit of keeping the precepts is one and the same; therefore one should only praise one another and not wound one another. The Vimalakīrti Sutra says: “Keep your own precepts; do not censure others' faults.” Only thus does one accord with the perfectly fused purport of the Buddha Dharma. If students do not understand this principle and go so far as to divide into factions and slander one another, that is truly to be lamented. Take the matter of vegetarianism: those who study the Great Vehicle say that the Small Vehicle's vegetarianism is clinging to marks, and those who study the Small Vehicle say that the Great Vehicle's not abstaining from meat is contrary to the Buddha Dharma, and they reproach one another in confusion. You should know that eating vegetarian food cultivates a compassionate mind and gives up the pleasures of the palate, and truly has merit. But one of the Great Vehicle who does not abide in marks takes walking the bodhisattva path as his root; if he were confined to a vegetarian diet, how could he rely on the four means of gathering and carry out the functions of beneficial action and cooperation? Moreover the Buddha's regulations also permit eating the three kinds of pure meat as a skillful means — how could abstaining or not abstaining from meat be enough to determine whether something is the Buddha Dharma or not?

Again, take the matter of abstaining from sexual conduct: this is the most important precept for a student of the Buddha Dharma. The Small Vehicle bodhisattva abstains for life, which is indeed the root of escaping birth and death; but the Great Vehicle bodhisattva, whose mind does not abide in marks yet is not apart from marks, cuts off only sexual misconduct and need not cut off all marital relations. Why? Because the bodhisattva manifests according to capacity and mingles with the world and blends with the light, and only so can he gather all in. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius came into the world in response to the times, and all were bodhisattvas. In the age of the Dharma's ending, bodhisattvas appear even in brothels and among butchers. Only, the bodhisattva does not fall into wrong views: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying he must do for the sake of saving the world and benefiting living beings. The Tathāgata himself also showed that he had a wife and child, precisely to reveal right view. If everyone in the world abstained from sexual conduct, how could a bodhisattva enter the world? How could he fulfill the vow that until all living beings are saved he will not be saved? It is for this reason that the bodhisattva retains affliction to moisten his rebirth. Moreover the bodhisattva manifests all kinds of contrary conduct, which ordinary beings cannot fathom.
