Thus this six-syllable great bright mantra, though earnestly sought by Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, was transmitted by a Dharma master who had broken the precepts and had a wife and children, as recorded in the Sutra of the Great, Precious, Adorned King of the Great Vehicle. And in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Tathāgata answered Maitreya Bodhisattva's question about how many kinds of skillful means there are for returning into the dust of toil, saying plainly that one enters the world by the skillful means of great compassion, manifesting all kinds of forms and circumstances of opposition and accord, and cooperating with others. He also answered Bodhisattva Samantabhadra's question about what kind of person the living beings of the age of the Dharma's ending should seek and what kind of Dharma they should rely on. First he said: seek one of right knowledge and right view, whose mind does not abide in marks and does not cling to the realm of the hearers or the solitary realizers, who though manifesting in the dust of toil keeps his mind forever pure, who shows various faults yet praises the pure life. And again he said: he manifests all kinds of faults and troubles, yet his mind is without arrogance — how much less does he grasp at wealth, wife, and children! From this one sees that in practicing the Great Vehicle Dharma one must not cling to marks. But though the bodhisattva manifests contrary conduct, in every case there is the deed and no the mind. If the mind is not pure, and one has some other design, using as a pretext the non-clinging to marks and the manifestation of contrary conduct to shield one's shortcomings, and boasting that one is a Great Vehicle bodhisattva practicing the Great Vehicle Dharma gate — such a person truly holds wrong views and must fall into the Avīci hell, for causality is never destroyed.

The Buddha Dharma certainly gives weight to understanding and awakening, but gives even more weight to practice and realization. Yet without practice one cannot attain realization; therefore the Sixth Patriarch said: “To hear, see, and recite is the Small Vehicle.” For one who merely displays much learning only increases his views; seeing a dharma he is moved, and clinging to objects he gives rise to thoughts — hence it is called the Small Vehicle. To awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the Middle Vehicle. For the meaning of the Buddha Dharma is very deep and hard to know, and one who can awaken to and understand it also has merit; but since he cannot practice and realize according to the Dharma, it is called the Middle Vehicle. To practice according to the Dharma is the Great Vehicle. For every dharma is equal and fundamentally there is no great or small; all dharmas take practice as their root. Whoever can practice according to the Dharma, unchanging to the end, will certainly accomplish it — hence it is called the Great Vehicle. To penetrate all dharmas thoroughly, to be complete with all dharmas, to be defiled by nothing, to be apart from all marks of dharma, and to attain nothing whatsoever — this is called the supreme vehicle. For such a one is in marks yet apart from marks, and the mark of reality is markless; therefore he is not defiled or attached, and also attains nothing. Markless and non-attaining is also called truly attaining. He penetrates all dharmas and is also complete with all dharmas; it cannot be spoken of, and only realization knows it. Hence it is called the supreme vehicle. Among these four vehicles, the first three, though they involve speech, cannot be truly known without personal realization. Therefore practicing according to the Dharma is the root of the student of the Buddha Dharma. If one receives the Dharma but does not practice it, or practices but not according to the Dharma, it is hard to attain realization and nothing is accomplished.

Whatever school a student of the Buddha Dharma may practice, he is a disciple of the Buddha. But if one does not rely on one's own method and practice it earnestly, burying oneself in the work, and instead only reproaches others and discriminates great from small, then the Buddha Dharma declines to this degree — worse than the Catholicism and Protestantism of the Westerners, which at least attain the human and deva paths. Why? Whatever their doctrine may be, let us set it aside; yet their old and new believers can each carry forward the spirit of their Old and New Testaments, spreading it everywhere, shrinking not from the toil of climbing mountains and crossing seas, enduring hardship and bitterness. Wherever they arrive, they exhaust their wit and strength and do not stop until they have established a church. Having established it, they go on to open schools and set up hospitals and every kind of charitable work. Look at those who today are very rich and very famous — many of them were nurtured by these churches. Such spirit and such conduct, though it be a small fruit of the human and deva paths and a cause with outflows, is still enough to inspire belief. If we shut our eyes and think, are we not ashamed? And still we shut the door and flatter ourselves, and even reproach one another! You should know that the Buddha Dharma is fundamentally without contention; to contend is to lose the meaning of the Way, and to lose the meaning of the Way is to go against the Buddha's intent. To destroy the Buddha Dharma — is that to be a disciple of the Buddha?

If the disciples of the Buddha's gate wish the Buddha Dharma to flourish, they should remove the strife of factions and each rely on his own method and keep his own precepts. Whether bodily precepts or mind precepts, if one can keep them, that is the right way; if one cannot keep them, that is not the right way. The Sixth Patriarch said: “If you would see the true Way, right conduct is the Way.” When the ancients made the character zheng, right, it was composed of “one” over “stop,” concealing a meaning of teaching and transformation. According to the Buddha Dharma, all Dharma gates return to non-duality; to stop at one is right, to have two is not right. When word and deed are not two, that is one; when word and deed are not one, that is two. Rightness requires that the mind be right; if the appearance is right but the mind is not right, one is still not a true disciple of the Buddha. If one's own mind can be right, then good and bad are equal. Being equal, praise and blame are left to others — why take account of them? When the Buddha was in the world there were still those who slandered him; how much more afterward! And slander can dissolve karma — why be afflicted by it? Slander is of two kinds: deliberate and unintentional. Whoever slanders deliberately has some other purpose, and need not be discussed. The unintentional slanderer does not understand the principle clearly, and is even less worth taking account of. We who practice the mind-ground Dharma take benefiting others and no-self as our vow — what slander is there for us? Moreover the fundamental principle of the Esoteric Dharma is to take the bodhi mind as cause and great compassion as root. Understanding this, all words of slander are no different from sweet dew!

Fellow students, the Buddha spoke of four vehicles — but how could there be four? It is the so-called one road of the nirvāṇa gate, with no great or small. Therefore the Lotus Sutra opened the provisional and revealed the real, and the Tathāgata himself said that the Dharma is only one vehicle, with no second and no third. And the four great hearers all received the Buddha's prediction, which shows all the more that there is no great or small. The Sixth Patriarch said that vehicle means practice: one whose measure of mind is great performs great practice; one whose measure of mind is small performs small practice. As it is said, “In poverty, one cultivates oneself alone; in prosperity, one benefits all under heaven.” The two words poverty and prosperity need not be interpreted as low and high station. The poor in mind are poor, and being poor in mind their measure is small; the accomplished in mind are accomplished, and being accomplished in mind their measure is great. After teaching at Deer Park, the Tathāgata saw that the hearers' measure of mind was too small and that they still clung to marks, and so he sent them to Vimalakīrti's chamber to be rebuked, so that their measure of mind might become great and they might rise up in great practice. From this one may know that it is not one who practices the Great Vehicle Dharma who is thereby a Great Vehicle. Only one whose wisdom is great, whose measure of mind is great, whose vow and practice are great, whose merit is great, and who clings to no marks at all, counts as the Great Vehicle. Though one practices the Great Vehicle Dharma, if his wisdom is small, his measure of mind small, his vow and practice small, his merit small, and he clings to marks everywhere, he is still the Small Vehicle. What is great? When the mind-ground is without wrong, the essence is great; when one benefits others without self, the function is great. Let each of you base himself on the essence and function of these two phrases and practice them earnestly without clinging to the marks of practice; only then will you be worthy of studying this mind-ground Dharma. But where, after all, should one practice? You should know that one must practice in both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. The Sixth Patriarch said: “The Buddha Dharma is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world. To seek bodhi apart from the world is like seeking a hare's horn.” Through many kalpas you have practiced, and so you now study this markless mind-ground Dharma — an excellent condition not to be missed through negligence, and do not discriminate great from small. I, Huiming, have already said in my recorded sayings: “The wisdom of non-discrimination is supreme wisdom.”

blocks.text: Thirteenth Sitting: Abiding Nowhere, Arousing the Mind

inline.s: Fellow students, the two lines of sutra, “One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere,” are the most important critical juncture in the Diamond Sutra; let me say a little about them. The Diamond Sutra is the prajñā of the mark of reality, spoken by the Buddha for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle mind and for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind; it can open the student's great wisdom. But the whole of the Diamond Sutra breaks marks to reveal the essence. The two lines “One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere” reveal essence and function together. What are essence and function? “Abiding nowhere” is the essence, “giving rise to that mind” is the function; function is not apart from essence, essence is not apart from function. “Abiding nowhere” does not fall into existence, and “giving rise to that mind” does not fall into nothingness — only this is the true purport of the Diamond. Therefore when the Sixth Patriarch heard these two lines he awakened to the Way at once. But why did the Sixth Patriarch awaken as soon as he heard them? You should know that the Sixth Patriarch was a bodhisattva in a fleshly body and had long since seen the nature. Why? Look at the Sixth Patriarch's verse: “Bodhi is fundamentally no tree; the bright mirror is also not a stand. Originally there is not a single thing; where could dust ever cling?” From this verse the Fifth Patriarch knew that the Sixth Patriarch had already awakened to the essence of the nature that abides nowhere, but had not yet understood the wonder of arousing the mind and rising up in function; therefore he had him come into his room at the third watch. When he transmitted the sutra to the two lines “One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere,” the Sixth Patriarch greatly awakened to the principle that essence and function are not two. Afterward he taught and transformed students by this, and greatly revived the school's spirit. From this one sees that these two lines of sutra are very important, and I hope you will pay special attention to them.

Abiding nowhere” means abiding in nothing at all. If one can abide in nothing at all, that is the realm of the mark of reality. Having awakened to the truth that the mark of reality is markless and that nothing is attained, what self-clinging, affliction, birth and death, or ignorance is there to abide in? But if one clings to abiding nowhere, one falls again into one-sided emptiness. Why? You should know that true emptiness is not empty. How is it not empty? Empty and still, numinously knowing, it rises up in function and shows itself. How does the function rise? It rises by giving rise to that mind according to prajñā wisdom. How does one give rise to the mind? One gives rise to the wonderful luminous true mind that we originally possess — that is, one gives rise to the bodhisattva mind of inexhaustible compassionate vow, the bodhi mind, the mind of compassion, the mind of equality, the mind of benefiting others without self. Minds such as these are all minds arising from abiding nowhere, and they are the true mind, the pure mind, which is also the Buddha mind. But the minds that living beings give rise to are the mind of greed, the mind of self-clinging, the mind of arrogance, the mind of discrimination, and on to the eighty-four thousand minds of affliction. Minds such as these are all minds arising from abiding in something, and they are the deluded mind, the karmic consciousness mind, which is also the mind of living beings. Why? Because living beings cling to marks everywhere; with many marks the mind is many too, and with a mind that is many it cannot be pure, and with an impure mind one cannot awaken to the true mind of the mark of reality. Therefore if a student of the Buddha Dharma wishes to awaken to the true mind of the mark of reality, he must put everything down; then he abides nowhere, the true mind appears of itself, and that is the mind of the Way. The Way is born of the mind, and the mind is seen through the Way. Speaking to the ultimate, this one word “Way” also cannot be spoken of. As it is said, the path of speech is cut off and the road of mental activity is extinguished. This principle is subtle, and the beginner cannot easily apprehend it. The Buddha wanted people to apprehend that the mark of reality is markless and that freedom from thought is the true mind, and so he said, “One should abide nowhere.” The Buddha also wanted people to apprehend the wonder of rising up in function, and so in skillful means he said, “and give rise to that mind.” The two lines, “One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere,” seem to feel contradictory, but in fact they are just so.

Fellow students, since you know that abiding nowhere is markless bodhi, and is also the realm of the dharmakāya Buddha, do not go seeking this mark of reality or this dharmakāya Buddha — to seek is not it. Why? The mark of reality is markless and cannot be sought. To put it down is to be it; to stir a thought is to be wrong. As soon as the mind of seeking arises, it becomes deluded thought. You should know that this realm of the mark of reality is not the exclusive possession of the buddhas; we too are originally complete with it. Why? Because Buddha and living being are fundamentally not two. If only you will close your eyes in still illumination at this moment, with not one thought arising, then thus and unmoving, one body with all things, that is the true mind that abides nowhere, the mark of reality. If one thought stirs ever so slightly, that is abiding in something. Abiding in something is not the mark of reality. Therefore the ancient worthy said: “When not one thought arises, the whole appears; as soon as the six senses stir, it is covered by clouds.” Those whose practice does not correspond do so because they abide in something and therefore seek something; abiding and seeking is to bind oneself up — how can one then see one's own nature?

What you are now practicing is the mind-ground Dharma, and you must see clearly the principle of “abiding nowhere and giving rise to that mind.” To understand the essence and function of these two lines of sutra, one must first establish the essence, and only then can one rise up in function. How is the essence established? Put down all minds that seek and abide, and it is established. For when everything is put down, the deluded mind ceases of itself. When the deluded mind ceases, the true mind that abides nowhere naturally appears. But though you know clearly that putting down is good, you still cannot put it down — why? Because our karmic consciousness is too deep and putting down is not easy. Since putting down is not easy, one must begin from subduing the mind. You little realize that abiding in nothing at all is itself the subduing. If one seeks subduing elsewhere, that is adding a head on top of a head. If one can truly abide in nothing, one attains the essence of the mark of reality. Based on the essence of the mark of reality, to abide in what is not abided in and to arouse what is not aroused is to rise up in function according to the essence.

The difference between Buddha and living being lies only in awakened and unawakened, compassionate and uncompassionate. Awakened, one is in marks yet apart from marks and abides in nothing at all, and so is called Buddha; unawakened, one sees objects and gives rise to thoughts and abides in everything, and so is called a living being. Compassionate, one embraces all equally and all things are one body, and so is called Buddha; uncompassionate, one is full of greed, hatred, delusion, and arrogance, and affliction springs up in profusion, and so is called a living being. Yet awakened and unawakened are a distinction in essence; compassionate and uncompassionate are a difference in function. Essence and function are not two, and both are one mind. If one can turn an evil mind into a good mind, that is the Buddha mind. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch said: “With a single thought of evenness and directness, a living being is Buddha.”

Fellow students, the Buddha has three bodies, and you should know that we too have three bodies: the dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya. When it does not abide, the true mind that is empty, still, and numinously knowing, pervading space, is the dharmakāya. When it gives rise to the mind, good thoughts giving rise to good reward and evil thoughts to evil reward, the mind at that time is the saṃbhogakāya. A single thought of calculation and all kinds of transformation: thinking evil transforms into hell, thinking good transforms into heaven — the mind at that time is the nirmāṇakāya. If you understand this principle, you should work at every moment on abiding nowhere and arousing the mind. Let the mind be like space, yet not dwell on the measure of space; save all beings, yet cling to no mark of any being. As it is said, follow conditions without changing, and be unchanging while following conditions: unchanging is abiding nowhere, following conditions is arousing the mind.

blocks.text: Fourteenth Sitting: Transcending the World and Entering the World

inline.s: Fellow students, the true principle of the Buddha Dharma cannot in itself be spoken, and transcending the world and entering the world are also provisional names. Let me speak in skillful means: both return to one mind. Ultimately, which mind transcends the world and which mind enters it? You should know that the true mind transcends the world and the deluded mind enters it. Transcending the world is the Buddha Dharma; entering the world is worldly dharma. Transcending the world is emptiness; entering the world is existence. Transcending the world is the dharmakāya; entering the world is the saṃbhogakāya. Transcending the world is true; entering the world is false. Yet the true and the false are not one, and apart from entering the world there is no transcending it. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch said that apart from the world there is no bodhi. This principle must be investigated with the mind before one knows the Tathāgata's compassionate response to the world and the great matter of his appearing.

The beginner in the Buddha Dharma speaks only of transcending the world and not of entering it. But one who is ignorant of the Buddha Dharma speaks only of entering the world and does not know transcending it. Both fall into extremes. Why? Worldly dharma is the Buddha Dharma; apart from the false there is no true, and apart from the true there is no false. Moreover the true principle of the Buddha Dharma is that entering the world is transcending it, and transcending it is entering it. Therefore the sutra says: “The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.” It also says: “Thus and unmoving.” You should know that transcending the world and entering it are the principle of essence and function not being two. Transcending the world is the essence, entering the world is the function; apart from the essence there is no function, apart from the function there is no essence. Such is the true principle of the Buddha Dharma. But ordinary beings deludedly give rise to discrimination: clinging to entering the world, they give rise to confusion and create karma; clinging to transcending the world, they loathe and leave birth and death. They little realize that all dharmas are like illusions and that birth and death cannot be found either. To break such clinging the Tathāgata complied with living beings and manifested all kinds of skillful means to lead them into the Way. In truth he responds where there is no response and abides where there is no abiding. His dharmakāya true mind pervades the ten directions and its wonderful function is thus — precisely expressing transcending the world. And his saṃbhogakāya, based on this true mind, manifests an illusory body and transforms according to capacity — precisely expressing entering the world. If a student of the Buddha Dharma understands this principle, then abiding where there is no abiding and arousing what is not aroused, neither abiding nor arousing, is the true mind. The true mind is emptiness, the deluded mind is existence; in all things, having the deed and no the mind, one is at ease at once — where is there any going out or coming in? But this principle is subtle and beginners cannot easily apprehend it; therefore one must work on abiding nowhere and arousing the mind. Hence the sutra says: “One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.” Abiding nowhere is transcending the world; arousing the mind is entering the world. Abiding nowhere and arousing the mind is the wonderful mind in which transcending and entering the world are not two.

The Great Vehicle Buddha Dharma is not apart from entering the world and does not abandon transcending it; therefore it puts first the cultivation of the mind. That one's practice does not correspond is not because the Buddha Dharma does not correspond, but because the student will not work on the mind, and so does not understand the mind-ground. Not knowing which mind is true and which is false, not knowing that the true mind and the deluded mind are one mind, and still less knowing that the wonder of the one mind cannot be found either — therefore the practice does not correspond. When practice does not correspond, the work is not accomplished and the function is not revealed. For if the true principle of the Buddha Dharma cannot be awakened to, other principles too are hard to fathom thoroughly, and so the world's ways suffer. You should know that the decline of the world's ways is not because worldly dharmas are bad, but because people's minds are not right. Why? When people's minds are not right, the mind of the Way is not established, and so they abandon the true and chase the false, abandon the root and chase the branches, follow the current and forget to return; the true principle grows dimmer and the world's ways decline the more. Therefore it is said that things depend on human effort and the Way depends on human practice, and that worldly dharma and Buddha Dharma are not two in principle. Hence the Confucians say: “Cultivate the person by the Way; cultivate the Way by benevolence.” If everyone could base himself on a benevolent mind and do benevolent deeds, at home being kind and filial, abroad being loving and forgiving, moving benevolence by benevolence and overcoming the unbenevolent by benevolence, why fear that the world's ways are unbenevolent?

Recently people, seeing the nation's weakness, have come to doubt that the inherited culture is of any practical use. In truth Chinese culture is the highest, and its morality is supreme. The Confucian cultivation of self, regulation of the family, ordering of the state, and pacifying of the world has already reached the utmost in the way of entering the world, while the Great Vehicle Buddha Dharma encompasses all and saves all beings, and the two proceed without conflict. Only, in modern times, as European culture spread eastward, learning has been new, but people are deluded by materialism and neglect idealism, knowing only how to enter the world and not how to transcend it. And our countrymen, dazzled by utility, mostly will not study the inherited culture deeply, so that people's minds decline like a river day by day and the world's ways grow ever shallower. If one would save the world's ways, one must first save people's minds. To save people's minds, one should urgently propagate the Buddha Dharma. Why? The Buddha Dharma is boundless: it does not abide in the unconditioned and does not cling to the conditioned; it does not abandon transcending the world and is not apart from entering it; it leans neither to idealism nor to materialism. With the true mind that all dharmas are without self it employs all dharmas; with the measure of mind of all compassion it deals with all people. In this way all things find their place, and transformation is accomplished of itself. Here is a verse to reveal the essentials.
Buddha Dharma, worldly way — from the first not two, but one, I say.
A mind of good is bodhi bright; a mind of evil, a yakṣa's night.

The Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha Dharma, and also says that by practicing all good dharmas one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. From this one sees that the Buddha Dharma is not apart from worldly dharma, and that the only difference lies in good and not good. But dharmas have no self-nature; good and not good rest wholly in the one mind. When the mind is right, the dharma is good; when the mind is crooked, the dharma is not good. With a mind that transcends the world and is without self, performing the work of entering the world to benefit others, all dharmas are good dharmas, and good dharmas are bodhi. Otherwise, all dharmas are not good dharmas, and what is not a good dharma is a yakṣa.

In the science of Europe and America, which leans toward the material, good and not good are likewise so. Insofar as it provides the means of living and the crafts, and benefits humankind, it is bodhi. Insofar as it produces novel weapons of war that poison and harm living beings, it is no different from a yakṣa. Yet the original intent of those who invented such weapons was to benefit society and the nation; they did not think of the harm to the peoples of the world, so that the matter grew worse and worse and came to contradict the original intent of the invention. You should know that to create the cause of killing people day after day must bring the fruit of being killed by people, and the misery to come can be imagined. Tracing the cause, it lies in one-sidedly clinging to the conditioned function of entering the world while neglecting the unconditioned essence of transcending it. To have function and no essence is to lean to one side and lose balance. The reason they cling to entering the world and neglect transcending it is that they think the unconditioned falls into emptiness, and that it is better to have the conditioned give rise to the ten thousand existents. In truth emptiness and existence are not two: for example, all living things cannot be born apart from space, nor grow apart from earth. Heaven gives birth and earth gives growth — this precisely reveals the function of emptiness and existence not being two. Therefore to cling one-sidedly to existence, though its efficacy may flourish for a time, will, when things reach their extreme, reverse itself, and in the end it is no policy for lasting peace. Chinese culture is originally very high, and the principle of growth and decline pervades people's minds. Thus those of idealist bent, loathing the harm of materialism, lean toward spirit. They little realize that to lean toward matter is certainly to cling to existence, but to lean toward spirit is also to cling to emptiness. To cling to existence or to cling to emptiness are both not the middle way. You should know that spirit is the essence and matter is the function. If there is essence and no function, all that is discussed is useless learning; if there is function and no essence, all that is done is work without essence. Useless learning and work without essence are equal in their harm. Therefore in these circumstances, besides actively enlarging the inherited moral culture, one should on the one hand use spirit to employ matter, and on the other develop a beneficial science, using matter to bring spirit to radiance — only thus does one accord with the meaning of the middle way.

Worldly people think that a student of the Buddha Dharma should not speak of worldly dharmas, and that to speak of them is like driving in reverse. You should know that the reverse car is the forward car. Why? Every dharma is perfectly fused, mutually containing and mutually embracing. Entering the world certainly contains transcending it, and transcending the world is not apart from entering it. Entering and transcending the world are still provisional names; reverse car and forward car are even more a play of words. Therefore the sutra says: no fixed dharma can be spoken of. In sum, the true principle of the Buddha Dharma is not apart from worldly dharma, and transcending the world and entering it rest wholly in one's own mind. When the mind is right, entering the world is also transcending it; when the mind is not right, transcending the world is also entering it. The Sixth Patriarch said: “Right view is called transcending the world; wrong view is called the world.” I, Huiming, have limited awakening; what I offer in skillful means is only for you to take as a reference.

blocks.text: Fifteenth Sitting: Existence and Non-Existence Are Not Two

inline.s: Fellow students, that mind is Buddha is not valued for being spoken of; that existence and non-existence are not two is even less to be spoken of. Let me speak of it in skillful means. Ultimately, which mind is Buddha — the conditioned mind or the unconditioned mind? What is the conditioned mind? It is the mind of arising and ceasing. What is the unconditioned mind? It is the mind of true suchness. If one says the conditioned mind is Buddha, then the conditioned mind is the deluded mind of arising and ceasing, the mind of ordinary beings — how can it be called Buddha? If one says the unconditioned mind is Buddha, then the unconditioned mind is the wonderful mind of true suchness, like space, originally markless and utterly ungraspable; being markless and ungraspable, which is Buddha? You should know that minds such as the conditioned and the unconditioned are fundamentally not two. The mind that is not two is one's own mind, and this is called Buddha. Why? All the ten thousand dharmas are manifested by the one mind of true suchness. Our deluded mind is fundamentally the true mind. Therefore the permanently abiding true mind is the essence of the deluded mind of arising and ceasing, and the deluded mind of arising and ceasing is the function of the permanently abiding true mind — hence it is called not two. The dharmakāya is the essence, the saṃbhogakāya is the function. Dharmakāya and saṃbhogakāya are originally one body. True mind and deluded mind return to one mind. Only, our true mind and dharmakāya are unconditioned, while the deluded mind and saṃbhogakāya are conditioned. The unconditioned is the essence, the conditioned is the function. Function is not apart from essence, essence is not apart from function. Hence it is called not two.

In the Buddha Dharma, the gate of true suchness, neither arising nor ceasing, is the unconditioned; the gate of arising and ceasing, with arising and ceasing, is the conditioned. But to speak of existence and non-existence, of arising and ceasing, of neither arising nor ceasing, is all skillful means of remedy. You should know that arising and ceasing falls into existence; neither arising nor ceasing falls again into non-existence. The true suchness of the original mind arises yet does not arise, ceases yet does not cease; that is true suchness unchanging, unchanging true suchness, and it can be called neither existent nor non-existent. Xue Jian asked the Sixth Patriarch: “How does neither arising nor ceasing differ from the outer paths?” The Patriarch said: “To use cessation to stop arising and to use arising to manifest cessation is the teaching of the outer paths. What I call neither arising nor ceasing is fundamentally without arising and now also without ceasing — not the same as the outer paths.” This principle is subtle and profound and by no means easy to know; let me take the bright mirror as a figure.

The substance of the mirror is originally bright: this figures true suchness. Its brightness can reveal colors: this figures arising and ceasing. When the mirror reflects an object, the bright substance does not move: reflecting red it shows red, reflecting green it shows green. When it reflects red, though red appears, the mirror is not dyed red. When it reflects green, though green appears, the mirror is not dyed green. Showing red and showing green is arising and ceasing. Yet though there is arising and ceasing, the substance of the mirror does not move. The substance that does not move is true suchness. When the color leaves the mirror, the mirror keeps no color: that is the previous thought not arising. When the next color comes to the mirror, the mirror shows color again: that is the later thought not ceasing. If the previous thought does not arise and this very body is empty and still, then once self-clinging is broken the true mind that abides nowhere appears before one — that is being without wrong and without self. If the later thought does not cease, then true emptiness is not empty, and rising up in function from the essence, one gives rise to that mind from abiding nowhere — that is benefiting others without self. The mirror's ability to reflect and reveal is the benefiting of others of arising-and-ceasing that does not cease; the mirror's not being dyed and not keeping is the being-without-wrong of non-arising and non-ceasing. True suchness and the mirror are one principle, not two. When things come it responds; when matters go it keeps nothing. Bright and at ease, its function is thus. It follows conditions without changing and is unchanging while following conditions. But when the mirror is covered with dust, its brightness does not appear, and though an object is before it, it cannot reflect it. If it is rubbed, then when the dust is cleansed the brightness returns at once. So too with living beings: karmic obstructions cover the true suchness of the original mind, so that the true and the false are inverted. If one arouses the aspiration and practices truly, then karmic obstructions dissolve and the true mind appears again. True suchness and the mirror are fundamentally not two in principle; rubbing and practice are the same in fact. Therefore the ultimate wisdom is called the great perfect mirror wisdom.

Again take heaven and earth as a figure: the substance of heaven is fundamentally empty — that is the unconditioned, the same as true suchness and the dharmakāya. Earth gives rise to all things — that is the conditioned, the same as the deluded mind and the saṃbhogakāya. But if earth had not heaven's sun and moon to shine on it and rain and dew to moisten it, with their many wonderful functions, how could it grow all things? And if heaven had not earth's high plains and broad fields, its mountains, rivers, and hills, with all their complexity, how could it reveal the work of transformation and nurture? From this one may know that heaven and earth function for each other. Our unconditioned dharmakāya and conditioned saṃbhogakāya are just the same, and so they are not two.

Whoever becomes a Buddha, it is this deluded mind that is turned into the immeasurable true mind, which is the dharmakāya — it is not that the saṃbhogakāya is changed into the dharmakāya. Yet it is only from the saṃbhogakāya that one can cultivate to accomplishment, and so it is also not that one abandons the saṃbhogakāya and afterward can accomplish the dharmakāya. For the dharmakāya is unconditioned and the saṃbhogakāya conditioned; apart from the conditioned the unconditioned is not revealed, and all the conditioned is based on the unconditioned. Our false self is not apart from the true self; the deluded mind of living beings is not apart from the true mind. True self and false self are originally one self; deluded mind and true mind are one mind — hence it is called not two.

The Small Vehicle Buddha Dharma leans toward emptiness and stillness, because it clings to the unconditioned and loses the conditioned. To cling to one and lose the other is called two. The Great Vehicle Buddha Dharma benefits self and others, and so is called not two. The mind-ground Dharma takes the two phrases “a mind-ground without wrong” and “benefiting others without self” as essence and function. What are essence and function? A mind-ground without wrong is the essence; benefiting others without self is the function. If one does not establish the essence of a mind-ground without wrong, one certainly cannot rise up in the function of benefiting others without self. If one knows only the essence of a mind-ground without wrong and does not rise up in the function of benefiting others without self, then one has essence and no function and falls into the unconditioned. To cling one-sidedly to rising up in the function of benefiting others without establishing the essence of a mind-ground without wrong is to have function and no essence and to cling to the conditioned — neither is not two. One must establish the essence and enlarge the function, falling into neither existence nor non-existence, and only then is it called not two. Next, take light and darkness: without brightness, how could darkness be seen? And without darkness, how could brightness be revealed? Only when light and darkness function for each other — so too is benefiting others without self.

The Buddha says all dharmas are the mark of emptiness, and also says true emptiness is not empty; he says all existents are existent, and also says all existents are not existent; he says existence is illusion, and says illusion too is true; he says emptiness is true, and says emptiness too is illusion; he says all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; and he also says that by practicing all good dharmas one attains right and equal awakening; he speaks of the conditioned and then of the unconditioned; he speaks of transcending the world and then of entering it; he has taught the Dharma for forty-nine years and then says he has not uttered a single word; he speaks of immeasurable Dharma gates and then says they cannot be spoken of. Neither real nor unreal, both not and is — it is here that the principle of the Buddha Dharma is hard to know. Yet the true principle of the Buddha Dharma is true and not vain — how could it not be spoken of? If a practitioner begins to practice according to the Dharma, using the false to cultivate the true, and practices until true emptiness is wonderful existence and wonderful existence is true emptiness, so that the false becomes true and the unconditioned is realized — this is called the essence. Responding to the illusory with the true and manifesting the conditioned is called the function. To rise up in function according to the essence is to be in marks yet apart from marks: being in marks is the function, being apart from marks is Buddha. Based on this Buddha mind, one saves living beings according to conditions, clinging neither to the conditioned nor falling into the unconditioned. Conditioned and unconditioned are fundamentally not two, and all things are just so. Only because living beings cling too deeply — speaking of existence they cling to existence, speaking of non-existence they cling to non-existence, speaking of one they cling to one, speaking of two they cling to two — the Buddha therefore also taught that existence and non-existence are not two, speaking of the true and the false together, sweeping away as he spoke, to reveal non-duality. In truth all is provisional and skillful means to lead people in. Speaking to the return to the source, even the gate of non-duality cannot be spoken of. Why? The perfect wonderful one mind cannot even be found — how could it be spoken of? Formerly Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Vimalakīrti about the gate of non-duality, and Vimalakīrti was silent without a word. Mañjuśrī sighed: “Excellent, excellent! Even to be without words and letters — this is truly entering the gate of non-duality.” Such is the dharma of non-duality.

Fellow students, the Chan school is fundamentally without speech, and the Esoteric Dharma is even less to be spoken of. I, Huiming, am ashamed that my awakening to principle is not deep; earlier, because you asked again and again, I could not well go against your wishes, and at the start of the lectures I forbade any record; but you insisted, and I had to follow conditions. And fellow students in distant places, who did not come to hear, have again and again sent letters asking for a printed copy to read. This is not a king's banquet, yet you have the wish to share the food; I cannot stop it, and it only increases my shame. The fifteen talks given in all are no more than an offering for you to use as a temporary reference in practice; the principle is not profound and the words are coarse and common. If you insist on publishing them, I hope you will not print many copies, lest they circulate in the world and add to my offenses. In all Dharma gates, words are valued for conveying the meaning; if you can forget the words and take the meaning, then to speak is the same as not speaking, and to print is the same as not printing, and these spoken words are no more than waste paper. If you cling to the text and lose the meaning, then too to speak is the same as not speaking, and to print is the same as not printing, and these spoken words are also waste paper. If you understand that mind itself is Buddha, then no words are needed at all, and these spoken words become waste paper all the more. I hope each of you will give this thought three times over!

blocks.text: Appendix One: The Secret Essentials of Breaking Through the Gate

inline.s: If a student of the Buddha Dharma wishes to see his original face, he must break through the critical juncture of birth and death. To break through the critical juncture of birth and death, he must sweep away the evil habits of body and mind from beginningless time. To sweep away those evil habits, he must apply himself painfully to the work of keeping the precepts. When the work of keeping the precepts is deep, the evil habits gradually dissolve. Once they are wholly dissolved, the original nature appears of itself. But the mind precepts of the mind-ground Dharma have too high a mark, and are not easy to begin with. Therefore, to make it easier for beginners, a method is set out for gradually dissolving old habits, provisionally called breaking through the gate. Breaking through the gate has the same meaning as keeping the precepts, and further carries the sense of removing evil to the very end. The gate is a figure for evil karma; when evil is exhausted it is called broken through. Its chief items, gathered together, are eight: first, heart and mouth not one; second, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; third, double-tongued and harsh speech; fourth, greed, violence, and stinginess; fifth, hatred and jealousy; sixth, self-importance and slighting others; seventh, unstable faith; eighth, self-clinging and affliction. In these eight items the student should each embody the purport of bodily and mental precepts, and according to his own habits first remove the ones he easily commits and leave till last the ones he seldom commits. Having resolved, he should before the Buddha strictly make the vow to keep the precepts and break through the gate, and bitterly repent. To repent is to blame oneself for the past; to regret is to cut off the future. He should set a time limit and break through them one by one; either removing one kind within one period, or reforming several items in one period. The number should be carefully weighed and the length of the period set according to conditions. Within the time limit he must remove them wholly: the ones easily committed he no longer commits, and the ones seldom committed are then easily dissolved. This is the practical work of practice. If one cannot actually break through these coarse and heavy evil habits, then even the shallow Buddha Dharma is still beyond a wall for him — how could he enter deeply into the markless Dharma gate of a mind-ground without wrong and benefiting others without self?

blocks.text: Appendix Two: Buddha and Mara Are of One Mind

inline.s: The good and evil of human beings all arise from the mind. When the mind is good, one is a Buddha; when the mind is evil, one is a Mara. Buddha and Mara originally have no fixed nature; they simply shift according to the good or evil of one’s thoughts. Honesty, humility, compassion, and diligence are good thoughts; deceit, arrogance, hatred, and lustful indolence are evil thoughts. Thus when a single thought of goodness arises, the Buddha responds, and body, mind, and environment become harmonious and serene, so that one is transformed toward the Buddha. Not only does the good become ever better, but the wicked are also turned toward the good. When a single thought of evil arises, Mara responds, and body, mind, and environment turn harsh and base, so that one is transformed toward Mara. Not only does the wicked become ever worse, but the good are also turned toward the evil. Hence the saying, “Common beings and sages are within a single mind; good and evil are both wrought by the mind.” When the mind is Buddha, one is Buddha; when the mind is Mara, one is Mara; such is the inherent principle. In the age of the Latter Dharma most people are deluded and benighted, unable to tell good from evil, and so bring suffering upon themselves. Still worse are those who harbor crooked hearts while putting on fair words, thinking that all others can be deceived and that none in the world is as clever as they. Little do they know that baleful demons and evil spirits are already gathering upon their body and mind; once their karma is set in motion, at the least it brings illness, bereavement, and calamity, at the worst sinking them into the evil destinies. Even if past wholesome causes spare them for a while, once their merit is exhausted, retribution without end follows — how perilous! Such is the way in which doing good brings blessings and doing evil brings misfortune, and it has held true through the ages without ever failing. In short, Buddha and Mara never depart from one’s own mind. Why? Because everything is created by the mind alone. As the saying goes, when the mind arises all dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases all dharmas cease. Yet dharmas have no self-nature and are neither crooked nor upright: when the mind is right, even practicing a wrong dharma makes that dharma right; when the mind is wrong, even practicing the right dharma makes that dharma wrong. When the mind is good, Mara is turned into Buddha; when the mind is evil, Buddha is turned into Mara. In the very moment we set a thought in motion, how could we fail to be on our guard?!

blocks.text: Appendix Three: A Record of Master Huiming

inline.s: I recall that in the summer of the thirteenth year of the Republic I left the Wuchang Institute of Buddhist Studies for the second time and went to Guanghua Temple on Solitary Hill by West Lake in Hangzhou to found the monthly journal “Lion’s Roar” in order to promote a reform of Buddhism. I was betrayed by the abbot Zhenhao and suffered the combined blows of the local criminal element and the hostile forces about it, so the journal “Lion” was stillborn and I was unjustly held behind iron bars for more than ten days. Disheartened and weary, I took up quarters at Lingyin Temple in the recitation hall, gathering my mind and cultivating stillness, and in this way I was able to draw near to the eminent monk of his generation, the Elder Master Huiming. It happened that Katsuo-dera in Osaka, Japan, had opened an “Esoteric Buddhist Academy” and, under the banner of repaying the kindness of its source, was recruiting students from Chinese Buddhism free of charge. With the help of the Elder Master Huiming, toward the end of that year I invited the fellow residents, the two masters Tan Xuan of Hunan and Xiao Wu of Henan, to go there together to study.

To speak of the Elder Master Huiming, abbot of Hangzhou’s Lingyin Temple, there was no one from one end of the land to the other who did not know him, and he was especially praised by all the home-leaving Ch’an monks of every quarter. He was a native of Fujian and, I am told, left home in his youth. When I came to know him he was already an old man nearing seventy, short and slight, only a little over five feet tall, with bronze-colored skin, a striking head and high cheekbones, and a voice that boomed like a great bell. When he preached the Dharma in the main hall his voice set the temple’s bronze bell to humming, a sign of how extraordinary a man he was. To look at him, he resembled precisely the arhat who tames the dragon and subdues the tiger in the Arhat Hall, much like the bodily image of the Sixth Patriarch enshrined in the Patriarch Hall of Nanhua Temple in Guangdong.

The Elder Master Huiming had been a farmer in lay life and had never learned to read; after leaving home, all his labors were a life of ascetic practice. In the monastery he served in the outer offices, holding the hard-worn posts of vegetable cook, rice cook, water keeper, and cleaner, and in his spare time he delighted in sitting cross-legged and pondering Ch’an. How did this illiterate, toiling monk come to bear the honorific of a Dharma master? It is in truth something of a marvel. According to what the old-timers of the forests tell, when Master Huiming served as a server in the dining hall of Tiantong Temple in Ningbo — the duty of filling the bowls of the assembled community — he fed the dogs after every meal, and this counted as one of his daily routine tasks. He could not bear to throw away the rice the dogs had left; to cherish his blessings he would take it up, rinse it in water, and eat it himself. He did this for several years. One day, as he ate the rice the dogs had left, he suddenly burst into loud laughter. His fellow monks asked what he was laughing at. He said, “I have often heard people say that a dog has Buddha-nature. Today I understood this principle, and that is why I laugh.” From that time on it seems he had awakened into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is exactly what is meant by “the lowest of persons may hold the highest wisdom.”

After that, Tiantong Temple invited a master to lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. Although he was of the menial staff, he was most zealous, following the assembly every day to hear the sutra. One day he heard the master expound the passage, “The nature of perfect enlightenment is not a nature; in its nature it yet exists; it rises along with all natures, without grasping and without attaining,” and at once his mind opened and his understanding cleared, so that he suddenly beheld his own nature. After every lecture he would even set forth the meaning to his fellow monks, showing his grasp of the scripture. His fellow monks all mocked him, saying, “Look at your face in a mirror. With such a hard-bitten look and not a single character to your name, do you still fancy yourself a lecturer of the sutras?” Unable to contain his indignation, he answered, “Do you take me for one who cannot become a Dharma master? Very well, from today I am determined to become one just to show you, and in three years I shall return to Tiantong to lecture on the sutras! Just you wait and see!” When his fellow monks heard such big talk they all clapped their hands and laughed outright. Some said, “If a fellow of your stamp could become a lecturing Dharma master, then only when an iron tree puts forth blossoms and the waters of the Yellow River flow backward.” He said nothing further in dispute, but went straight back to his room, gathered up his robe and bedding, shouldered his bundle, and walked out of the monastery gate.

After leaving Tiantong he wandered about on foot everywhere, emulating Sudhana’s fifty-three visits, seeking out good teachers in every quarter, and making pilgrimages to the four great sacred mountains of China; before he knew it three years had passed. In the spring of the third year he heard that Tiantong Temple was again holding a sutra-lecture assembly, expounding the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment. The thought stirred in him, and he shouldered his bundle and came back to Tiantong. When he entered the guest hall and sat down, the guest master, seeing that he had only a shabby bundle, that he was short and small, and that he bore a hard-bitten look, took him for an ordinary wandering cloud-and-water monk. Putting on a stern face, he asked, “Master, what business have you at this monastery?” He answered, “I have come to hear the sutras and to beg an auditor’s seat of the temple.” The guest master thought to himself in amusement, “A toiler like you, and attend sutra lectures?” and so he teased him, “Do you know what sutra is being lectured on here?” He lifted his head and replied, “Why ever need you ask? Is it not the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment?” The guest master jested further, “And do you know how the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” are to be explained? Tell me; if you explain them aright, I shall grant you the seat.” Seeing that the guest master was deliberately putting him to the proof, he dropped his smile and, pointing at him, said, “How little you have studied! How can you ask about the Dharma with a flippant mind? If you would seek instruction from me, you must be reverent and respectful: don your robe, spread your sitting mat, prostrate yourself to me three times, and then kneel before me with palms joined; only then will I explain it to you. Is such a child’s-play attitude the way to seek the Dharma?” Smarting under this rebuke, the guest master felt that although the man’s appearance was unremarkable, he was by no means ordinary, and so he quickly made an apologetic bow, saying, “Very well, pray sit a moment; I shall be right back.”

That guest master turned and hurried to the abbot’s quarters, where he played upon the abbot a trick of “veiled deception,” saying that an unusual monk had just come to lodge there, that he declared himself come to hear the sutras and to beg an auditor’s seat, that when asked what sutra he wished to hear he had answered, the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment, and that when the guest master asked how the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” were explained, the monk’s tone was anything but humble, saying that the meaning of those three words could only be explained if the abbot himself donned his robe, took up his sitting mat, and invited him to the abbot’s quarters. When the abbot heard the guest master’s account, his curiosity was stirred, and he truly wrapped himself in his great crimson robe, took up his mat, and came to the guest hall, where he invited the monk Huiming to the abbot’s quarters. Once inside, the monk Huiming said to the abbot, “Venerable, if you would hear my words on the Dharma, you must lend me your Dharma seat.” The abbot agreed and respectfully installed him upon the seat. Seated there, he looked the very image of a Dharma master. He struck the block and began, “Venerable, the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” each admit four lines of explanation: within broad there is broad, within broad there is measure, within measure there is broad, and within measure there is measure. If I speak of the meaning of broad-within-broad, a whole lifetime would not see it done. To use the two lines of broad-within-measure and measure-within-broad would pass a year or half a year. But if I take up the line of measure-within-measure, I may discourse a while with you. I wonder which line the Venerable would care to hear?” Hearing this, the abbot realized this wandering monk was no simple person and dared not treat him lightly; he answered, “Pray, speak of measure-within-measure.” Thereupon he gave forth a great lion’s roar. What was meant by “great,” what by “square,” what by “broad” — he discoursed upon the threefold profound meaning of essence, character, and function of these three words, speaking freely from his own nature, like one whose bucket bottom had fallen out, pouring forth for a full three hours. The abbot, the more he listened, the more delighted he grew, feeling that every principle set forth flowed from the monk’s own self-nature, fell into no old ruts of the ancients, and was marked by original insight — inexhaustibly subtle and captivating. Straightway he prostrated himself in homage and, exclaiming again and again, “How excellent, Master! How excellent, Master!” begged him to lecture in his stead. This was the origin of the title of Dharma master by which the monk Huiming came to be honored, and the very first time he ever lectured on the sutras.

From that time on, monasteries in every quarter, admiring the fame of Master Huiming, vied to invite him to lecture, and at every lecture the seats were never empty. Though he had gained the name of a lecturing Dharma master, he did not labor over words and books; his interest lay in meditation. His lectures were delivered entirely from his own understanding, unlike other lecturing masters who relied on commentaries. He held that the principles in the commentaries were the views of earlier men and had nothing to do with himself; to recite the commentaries from memory was but to count another man’s treasure. So in lecturing he never classified doctrines, but only clarified the text and explained the meaning, delighting in the inspirational kung-ans and stories — and for this he was gladly heard by Ch’an monks and laymen and laywomen alike. As soon as word went out that Master Huiming was to lecture somewhere, the Ch’an monks and lay followers would stream after him, a sight never seen with ordinary lecturing masters. Though the Elder was a man who knew not a single character, the Dharma words he spoke were most refined. That year I spent the New Year at Lingyin; on New Year’s Eve he ascended the hall and spoke, and I recall two lines of his teaching: “Blossom by blossom the flowers bloom fair; petal by petal the plum leaves its fragrance.” How full of poetry! Could such words come from one who had never touched ink? Clearly they were the fruit of his enlightenment. (There is a volume of the Recorded Sayings of Master Huiming, set down by Master Tan Xuan of Hunan.)

In the half year I spent in the presence of the Elder Master Huiming, I felt this great worthy had many singular ways about him. The first was his distaste for vanity, and one fact proves it. In the 1920s, when Hangzhou’s Lingyin Temple was made an open ten-direction monastery (it had been a temple of a hereditary lineage), the elders of the surrounding monasteries and the supporting lay Buddhists of Hangzhou gathered to choose a first abbot. Esteeming Master Huiming’s deep attainment and weighty virtue, they all recommended the Elder as abbot of Lingyin, but he declined; though they pleaded with him again and again, he would not consent. After half a year they hit upon a stratagem: several noted local laymen came forward to invite the Elder to Lingyin Temple for a vegetarian meal, and suspecting no design, he accepted and went. The moment he stepped inside Lingyin’s mountain gate he saw monks standing in rows on both sides, all robed and holding their sitting mats, as if awaiting a great guest. Perceiving that things were amiss, he knew he had been tricked! At once he wheeled about and took to his heels. They gave chase, barred his way, and begged him to return. He thereupon sat himself on the ground, crossed his legs, and refused to rise at any cost. There was no helping it, so they lifted him and carried him back, bearing him into the Hall of the Heavenly Kings while the bells and drums sounded together and firecrackers were set off. He wept and cried out loudly; and even when they bore him to the abbot’s quarters and placed him upon the Dharma seat he would not stop wailing. The whole company knelt and cried in unison, “We congratulate the Venerable!” Weeping still, he said, “I am no material for an abbot. That you should all hold me so dear has in truth undone me. I have neither the Way, nor virtue, nor any practice whatever — what capacity have I to lead the assembly? Better choose some worthy one; I beg you all, in your compassion, to let me go!” And with that he fell to weeping again. Only when they all kneeled and pleaded, declaring they would not rise unless he consented, did the Elder reluctantly agree to stand in as abbot of Lingyin.

Although the Elder Master Huiming served as abbot of Hangzhou’s foremost monastery, a position and title so exalted, his whole manner of life yet remained as of old — still the bearing of a Ch’an monk. Every day he ate his meals in the hall with the community, partaking of no private dishes and sharing the very same grains of rice. In his bedroom there was nothing but a wooden frame bed; a single table stood in the room, and upon it was no ornament at all — only a teapot and a teacup. On the bed were only one worn cotton quilt, two tattered patched robes, and a set of old, worn spare underclothes. Even when devotees offered him new clothes, within a couple of days he would have turned them over to others. The band of rogue arhats of Hangzhou who had no clothes to wear and no money to spend would all come running to Lingyin to sponge off the Elder; and to these rogue arhats the Elder was most sympathetic, refusing none who came, answering every request, giving whatever was asked, never stinting.

The Elder Master Huiming was so full of compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and giving, and precisely because of this he got into no end of comical scrapes. He would go out and often come home transformed: either his great-sleeved outer robe was gone and he returned in only his short shirt and trousers, or his underclothes had been stripped off by the rogue arhats and he came back stark bare, wearing only the empty shell of his robe, pinching the hem between two fingers and walking home with an abashed look. Once the joke was worse still. The Elder, having gone early in the morning to a devotee’s house for an alms meal, was returning past the Broken Bridge at West Lake when he met a crowd of rogue arhats. The instant they saw him they pressed in all together, one begging for his outer robe, one for his jacket, one for his trousers. Smiling, the Elder satisfied them all, pulling off one garment after another and giving them over, until he was stripped wholly bare! He could not face anyone; it was most mortifying! Having no help for it, he jumped into the lake, sank his body beneath the water, and kept only his head above the surface, and so he soaked there until the sun was down behind the western hills, meaning to wait for darkness and slip away. Just then he caught sight of an acquaintance crossing the bridge, and called out to him, “My clothes are gone — I have given them all away in charity, and I cannot let myself be seen. Please hurry to the temple and send word; bid them bring me clothes at once.” In the end it was only when the temple sent someone with clothes and trousers that he climbed ashore. This old master was verily one who could “give up what is hard to give up.” Master Huiming gave away everything he had, and it became a treasured story of Hangzhou Buddhism.

The Elder Huiming was utterly of the common people, not given to luxury. The offerings that devotees ordinarily made him — fruit, sweets, cakes and pastries, and lengths of cloth — he never kept for himself, but at once sent attendants to the Ch’an hall, the recitation hall, and the hall for honored guests to be given away. When someone offered him a red packet, he would send the money to the storehouse to buy a meal for the community. He had a favorite catchphrase: “With all this entangling stuff lying about the room, I cannot sleep.” From this one may catch a glimpse of the old master’s freedom.

Though the Elder Huiming was a lecturing Dharma master and the foremost great abbot of a large monastery, he took no pride in his name and position, never swelled with self-importance, but was humble and approachable. His bearing was free and easy, like a spring breeze, warm and kindly; those of the pure community before him were seldom formal, and he delighted in mixing with them. Above all he felt closest to the ascetic monks of the menial offices, often chatting and joking with the hard-pressed vegetable cooks, gardeners, gatekeepers, and water keepers, and now and then helping plant vegetables, dig the ground, and carry slop — he would turn his hand to every kind of labor. In the seventeenth year of the Republic, when Mr. Chiang Kai-shek stepped down from power and went sightseeing at Lingyin Temple, drawn by the Elder’s spiritual bearing, he made a point of calling at the abbot’s quarters; he searched all about without finding him, until he went into the vegetable garden and there saw the Elder in a short shirt and tattered patched robe, holding a slop ladle and watering the vegetables. Mr. Chiang was charmed by his untrammeled manner, finding him frank and natural, never artificial, and so he stood in the garden conversing with him for a while.

The Elder Huiming’s bearing was always one of liberation. One year, Guiyuan Temple in Hubei invited him to lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. When the appointed day came, all the temple’s officers and monks lined up in ranks at the mountain gate to receive him. They waited and waited for three days, yet still he did not come, and all wondered at it. On the fourth day, as the abbot was eating in the dining hall, he noticed in a corner seat — the seat of a lodging monk — a master who looked very much like the Elder Huiming. Looking closely, he saw that it was indeed the very Elder Master Huiming who had been invited to lecture. Overjoyed, when the meal was finished the abbot announced from his seat that everyone should not retire to their rooms but receive the Elder Master Huiming right there in the dining hall. All were bewildered! Where was the Master Huiming? Why receive him in the dining hall? It was the abbot who rose from his seat and went to the honored guest’s place and drew the Elder forth. At a glance all knew the truth: this sutra-lecturing master had long since arrived at the temple and was hiding in the guests’ quarters! In fact he had come five days earlier, presenting himself as a lodging monk; the guest master had not recognized him and had sent him to the guests’ quarters. The abbot at once kneeled and prostrated himself in apology, and bade the guest master beg the Elder’s forgiveness. The Elder said, “The guest master is not to blame for the breach of manners. I feared to disturb the assembly and would not presume, so I myself chose to lodge as a guest; I was content with a guest’s life.” Surely we see how liberated the Elder Master Huiming was!

The Elder Master Huiming had one odd temper: all his life he hated women who rouged and powdered themselves, and he hated nuns who decked themselves out smartly. When he met such a nun he would pout and could not help but say a few satirical words: “You dress yourself so prettily because you are pleased to be looked at by others, so in your next life you are sure to be a woman again.” Consequently the young nuns of the nunnery circles in Hangzhou, the moment they caught sight of the Elder, would hurry away in fear and dare not face him. Nor did he make exception for the wives and daughters of great officials and noblemen; he was wont to let fall a few cutting remarks, caring not whether the hearer could bear them. Judge Guan Jiongzhi of the International Mixed Court in Shanghai was one of the most renowned lay patrons in Shanghai Buddhist circles. His concubine, decked out in all her finery, came to call on the Elder and was given a merciless dose of the stick and the shout. She went home and wept for three whole days. In the end she took the Elder’s words to be a Dharma teaching spoken in compassion, and was moved to shame instead; she changed into plain clothes, put aside her powder and rouge, and went again to pay her respects to the Elder, asking for his instruction and taking refuge under him as his disciple. Such were the doings of the eminent monks of old — what of the eminent monks of today?

Master Huiming passed away in the winter month of the nineteenth year of the Republic, and his relics were enshrined beneath a pagoda raised at that temple. In the thirty-fourth year, when the War of Resistance was won, I disbanded the monk rescue corps and came eastward downriver from the provisional capital, resting a second time at Lingyin Temple; the monastery posted a notice inviting me as “hall master,” and I dwelt in the quarters beside the pagoda holding the Elder’s relics for three years.
